chapters.title: Microbial Metabolism I: Catabolic Reactions for ATP synthesis

questions.stem: Of the 25 essential elements, _________ is a macronutrient and _________ is a micronutrient.

options.text: C/S
N/P
Fe/N
P/I
Se/Cu Carbon fixation: Light-independent reactions of photosynthesis

questions.answerRationale: Phosphorus is a macronutrient needed in bulk (nucleic acids, ATP, phospholipids); iodine is a trace micronutrient needed in only tiny amounts.

questions.stem: Which of the following reactions is showing carbon fixation?

options.text: C + O2 à CO2
CO2 + H2O àH2CO3
CH3COCOOH + CO2 à O2C-CH2COCOOH
CH3COCOOH + CoA + NAD+ à CO2 + CH3-CO-CoA + NADH + H+

questions.answerRationale: Carboxylating pyruvate with CO2 to form oxaloacetate incorporates inorganic carbon into an organic molecule - true carbon fixation - unlike simple oxidation, hydration, or a CO2-releasing decarboxylation.

questions.stem: In the Calvin cycle, which of the following reactions is catalyzed by the enzyme RuBisCo?

options.text: CO2 + Ribulose bisphosphate à 2 Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.
5 Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate à 3 Ribulose bisphosphate.
6 CO2 + 6 H2O à Glucose + 6O2.
H2CO3 à HCO3- + H+.

questions.answerRationale: RuBisCo catalyzes the actual carbon-fixing step of the Calvin cycle: combining CO2 with ribulose bisphosphate to form two molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.

questions.stem: Heterotrophs obtain their carbon from any of the following processes EXCEPT ________.

options.text: by predating
by parasitizing
by decomposing
through the Calvin cycle

questions.answerRationale: The Calvin cycle is how autotrophs fix their OWN carbon from CO2; heterotrophs by definition get organic carbon from other organisms instead - by eating, parasitizing, or decomposing them.

questions.stem: Challenge question. The land plants process about 123 billion tons of carbon (about 15% of the total atmospheric CO2) each year. How many tons of CO2 do the plants remove from the air, and how much CO2 is in the atmosphere? (Ref: Beer C et al. Science 2010; 329(5993):834-8). Note: The C atom accounts for 27.3% of the mass of CO2 molecules.

options.text: 45,000/ 300,000 Photosynthesis: Light-dependent reactions

questions.answerRationale: 123 billion tons C / 0.273 (C is 27.3% of CO2 mass) ≈ 450 billion tons of CO2 removed; since that is ~15% of total atmospheric CO2, the atmosphere holds roughly 450/0.15 ≈ 3,000 billion tons.

questions.stem: Which of these is a photosystem of a chloroplast?

options.text: Chlorophylls, phycobilin, phycoerythrin, phycocyanin, and carotenoids.
Light-harvesting antennae.
The reaction centers.
All these.

questions.answerRationale: A photosystem is the combined unit of light-harvesting pigments, the antenna complex that channels energy, and the reaction center that ultimately releases an electron - all three together, not any one alone.

questions.stem: All these components of a chloroplast may release electrons. Which of those electrons directly contributes to ATP synthesis?

options.text: Electrons released by water-plastoquinone oxidoreductase.
Electrons released by the photosystem II.
Electrons released by the photosystem I.
All these electrons.

questions.answerRationale: In the standard Z-scheme, electrons originating at water/PSII and those cycling through PSI/ferredoxin both ultimately drive proton pumping across the thylakoid membrane (directly or via cyclic photophosphorylation), so all of these electron flows end up contributing to the proton gradient that powers ATP synthase.

questions.stem: Which of these components of the thylakoid membrane of a chloroplast splits water and releases molecular oxygen?

options.text: PS I.
PS II.
WPO.
F0F1 ATP synthase.

questions.answerRationale: Photosystem II houses the water-splitting (oxygen-evolving) complex that pulls electrons from water and releases molecular O2.

questions.stem: Which of these makes the F0F1 ATP synthase of chloroplasts and mitochondria (or E. coli) different?

options.text: The substrate they use in ATP synthesis.
Dependence on proton gradient.
Structure of the enzymes.
None of these.
All these Nitrogen fixation

questions.answerRationale: F0F1 ATP synthase is a strikingly conserved enzyme across bacteria, mitochondria, and chloroplasts - same substrate (ADP+Pi), same chemiosmotic proton-gradient dependence, and largely the same core structure - so none of these listed properties actually differ between them.

questions.stem: If the cell runs out of nitrogen, which of the following molecules will the cell be able to synthesize?

options.text: Nucleotides.
Amino acids.
Sugars and lipids.
Proteins and nucleic acids

questions.answerRationale: Sugars and lipids are built from only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, so a cell can still make them without nitrogen - unlike nucleotides, amino acids, proteins, and nucleic acids, which all require nitrogen.

questions.stem: Only some bacterial species can fix atmospheric nitrogen. Which of the following bacterial genera are endophytic symbiotic diazotrophs?

options.text: Azospirillum.
Azotobacter.
Clostridium.
Rhizobium.

questions.answerRationale: Rhizobium is the classic nitrogen-fixing bacterium that lives symbiotically and endophytically inside legume root nodules, unlike the free-living diazotrophs Azospirillum, Azotobacter, and Clostridium.

questions.stem: Technically defined, which of the following is a nitrogen fixation reaction?

options.text: HNO3 + NaOH à NaNO3 + H2O.
2NO2 + O2 à 2 NO3-.
N2 + 3 H2 à 2 NH3.

questions.answerRationale: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 is the literal definition of nitrogen fixation: converting inert atmospheric N2 gas into a biologically usable form.

questions.stem: Bacteria generate 200 million tons, and humans generate 85 million tons of nitrogen compounds by fixing atmospheric nitrogen every year. Why do humans fix nitrogen?

options.text: Nitrogen compounds created by bacteria are inferior or not available to human use.
Nitrogen compounds produced by bacteria are not enough to meet current demand.
Nitrogen compounds created by bacteria are more expensive than those created by humans.

questions.answerRationale: Biological nitrogen fixation alone cannot produce enough usable nitrogen to meet the food-production demands of the modern human population, which is why industrial (Haber-Bosch) fixation supplements it.

questions.stem: Why is bacterial sulfur acquisition not considered sulfur fixation?

options.text: Because organic sulfur is abundant in soil.
Because sulfur compounds exist as solid chemicals, not as gases.
Because bacteria directly import sulfur compounds in soil capillaries.
Because absorbable sulfur compounds are already available in soil and water.

questions.answerRationale: Unlike inert atmospheric N2, absorbable sulfur compounds (sulfates, sulfonates) are already directly available for uptake in soil and water, so there is no inert gaseous form that needs to be "fixed" the way nitrogen does.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are an organic sulfur source in the soil and water?

options.text: Sulfate esters and sulfonates.
Elemental sulfur.
Iron sulfide.
H2S.

questions.answerRationale: Sulfate esters and sulfonates are organic sulfur compounds (sulfur bonded within organic molecules); elemental sulfur, iron sulfide, and H2S are all inorganic.

questions.stem: Which of these is an inorganic source of phosphorus?

options.text: Phytic acid.
Apatite ores.
Nucleic acids

questions.answerRationale: Apatite ores are a mineral (inorganic) source of phosphorus; phytic acid and nucleic acids are both organic phosphorus compounds.

questions.stem: Challenge question: If a cell runs out of phosphorus, which of these will the cell be unable to synthesize?

options.text: Lipids.
Proteins.
Nucleic acids.
Polysaccharides.
None of these molecules.

questions.answerRationale: Phosphate is structurally built into the nucleic acid backbone itself (the phosphodiester bond), making nucleic acids the molecule most directly and unambiguously impossible to synthesize without phosphorus.

questions.stem: Which of these organisms is an auxotroph?

options.text: It requires oxygen for cellular respiration.
It requires light energy to synthesize sugar.
It can synthesize all essential precursor molecules.
It cannot synthesize one or more essential precursor molecules.

questions.answerRationale: An auxotroph is, by definition, an organism that has lost the ability to synthesize one or more essential precursor molecules and must obtain them from its environment - the opposite of a prototroph.

questions.stem: Which of these is an essential amino acid for the human cell?

options.text: All 20 amino acids the cell needs for protein synthesis.
Hydrophobic amino acids (those insoluble in water).
Histidine, the human cell cannot synthesize it.
Arginine, the human cell can synthesize it.

questions.answerRationale: Histidine is one of the amino acids the human body cannot synthesize and must obtain from the diet; not all 20 amino acids are essential, and arginine being synthesizable by the cell would make it, by definition, NOT essential.

questions.stem: A cell has glucose but no erythrose (a tetrose sugar), which it needs at this moment. Which of these pathways will the cell use to produce it?

options.text: The Krebs cycle.
Gluconeogenesis
Glycolytic pathway.
Pentose-phosphate pathways.

questions.answerRationale: The pentose phosphate pathway's non-oxidative phase interconverts sugars of different carbon lengths (3- through 7-carbon), including producing 4-carbon erythrose-4-phosphate from glucose-derived intermediates.

questions.stem: Which of the following components may produce an amino acid in one step? Note: APS- adenosine phsophosulfate is AMP-SO4).

options.text: Glycerol and CO2.
Pyruvate and APS.
Acetyl-CoA and ATP.
An organic acid and ammonia.

questions.answerRationale: A one-step transamination or reductive amination reaction - an organic (keto) acid plus ammonia - directly yields an amino acid, unlike the other listed combinations.

questions.stem: If a cell were able to generate UMP, the cell would also be able to generate________.

options.text: UDP, GDP and CDP
UTP, CTP and dTTP
UMP, AMP and CMP Synthesis of template-independent macromolecules

questions.answerRationale: UMP can be phosphorylated to UDP then UTP, aminated to CTP, and reduced/methylated down the line to dTTP - all downstream pyrimidine nucleotides; the other options wrongly mix in purine nucleotides (GDP, AMP) that aren't reachable from UMP.

questions.stem: Which of these macromolecules are synthesized through a template-dependent manner?

options.text: The polypeptide chains of the peptidoglycan cell wall.
Phospholipids such as phosphatidyl ethanolamine.
Polysaccharides such as glycogen.
Chromosomal DNA.

questions.answerRationale: DNA replication is template-dependent, copying an existing strand base-by-base; peptidoglycan peptide chains, phospholipids, and glycogen are all assembled by dedicated enzymes without any template.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT necessary for the cell to synthesize glycogen?

options.text: An existing glycogen molecule.
NADH+H+.
Glucose.
UTP.

questions.answerRationale: Glycogen synthase builds glycogen from UDP-glucose onto an existing glycogen primer using glucose and UTP - none of which requires NADH as a cofactor.

questions.stem: Challenge question: Which of the following functions does the penicillin-binding protein (PBP) serve for bacterial cell wall synthesis?

options.text: Synthesis of NAG-NAM disaccharides.
Synthesis of the polypeptide chain attached to NAM.
Transport of NAG-NAM disaccharides to the periplasmic space.
Crosslinking the polypeptide chains of the NAM of two different polysaccharide chains.
Linking the NAG entity of a NAG-NAM disaccharide to a NAM entity of an existing polysaccharide molecule.

questions.answerRationale: Penicillin-binding proteins are the transpeptidases that catalyze the final crosslinking step, joining peptide chains between adjacent peptidoglycan strands - exactly what beta-lactam antibiotics block.

questions.stem: Which of these antibiotic groups do NOT interfere with bacterial cell wall synthesis?

options.text: Rifamycin.
Carbapenem.
Vancomycin.
Cephalosporin.

questions.answerRationale: Rifamycin inhibits RNA polymerase (transcription), not cell wall synthesis - unlike carbapenem, vancomycin, and cephalosporin, which all target cell wall assembly.

questions.stem: Grossly, which of the phases of the eukaryotic cell cycle is somewhat equivalent to the B period of the bacterial cell cycle?

options.text: S phase.
M phase.
G1 phase.
Interphase.

questions.answerRationale: The bacterial "B period" (gap before DNA replication begins) is roughly equivalent to the eukaryotic G1 phase, the gap before S-phase replication.

questions.stem: If a eukaryotic cell receives a mitogenic signal, the cell enters ______ and replicates DNA.

options.text: S phase
M phase
G1 phase
C period
D period Replication of chromosomal DNA

questions.answerRationale: A mitogenic signal pushes a eukaryotic cell out of G1 and into S phase, where DNA replication occurs.

questions.stem: Which of the following pieces of DNA would be replicated in a live E. coli?

options.text: Any dsDNA inserted in the cell.
The chromosome of a mitochondrion.
E. coli chromosome lacking the replicator.
The chromosome of a mitochondrion with the replicator of E. coli.

questions.answerRationale: What actually matters for E. coli's replication machinery is having a recognizable E. coli origin (replicator) sequence - attach that to otherwise foreign (even mitochondrial) DNA and the cell's initiator proteins will replicate it; DNA lacking a replicator, or of unrelated origin without one, will not be replicated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the last event for DNA replication initiation in E. coli?

options.text: A primase synthesizes an RNA primer.
Helicase loader loads DNA helicases on the ssDNA.
Initiator proteins bind the replicator of the chromosome.
The sliding clamp loader loads the sliding clamp and DNA polymerase III.

questions.answerRationale: Initiation runs: initiator proteins bind the replicator, the helicase loader loads helicases onto the exposed ssDNA, a primase synthesizes the RNA primer, and finally the sliding clamp loader loads the clamp and DNA polymerase III - the last event before elongation begins.

questions.stem: All the following items are events of DNA replication explained. Which of them is a mismatch (incorrect)?

options.text: Primases: Synthesize the RNA primer.
Helicases: Open dsDNA to create ssDNA.
Initiators: Bind the replication origin (replicator).
Topoisomerases: Bind ssDNA created by DNA helicases.

questions.answerRationale: Topoisomerases relieve torsional strain ahead of the replication fork by cutting and rejoining DNA strands - they do not bind the ssDNA that helicases expose; that job belongs to single-strand binding (SSB) proteins.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a substrate of DNA polymerase III of E. coli (i.e., which of these the DNA polymerase can use for the reaction it catalyses)?

options.text: The 3' OH end of the RNA or a DNA primer.
ATP, CTP, GTP and UTP.
dsDNA template.

questions.answerRationale: DNA polymerase III extends a strand from a free 3'-OH end (provided by an RNA or DNA primer); it uses dNTPs, not the ribonucleotides ATP/CTP/GTP/UTP, and copies single-stranded, not double-stranded, template.

questions.stem: DNA is being synthesized in an E. coli cell. Which of these is the leading strand?

options.text: The standard is being elongated in one small piece at a time.
The strand is made from many Okazaki fragments.
The strand is being continually elongated.
The bottom template strand.
The top template strand.

questions.answerRationale: The leading strand is synthesized continuously in the same direction as fork movement, unlike the lagging strand, which is made in discontinuous Okazaki fragments.

questions.stem: Which of these enzymes replicates most of the chromosomal DNA in E. coli?

options.text: Primases.
DNA ligases.
Topoisomerases.
DNA polymerase I
DNA polymerase III

questions.answerRationale: DNA polymerase III is the primary, highly processive replicase responsible for synthesizing the vast majority of E. coli's chromosomal DNA; DNA polymerase I only fills small gaps after primer removal.

questions.stem: Which of the following agents inhibits bacterial DNA replication by specifically inhibiting an enzyme?

options.text: Gamma radiation.
UV radiation.
Metronidazole.
Quinolones.
Busulfan.

questions.answerRationale: Quinolones specifically inhibit the bacterial enzyme DNA gyrase/topoisomerase; radiation and DNA-binding/alkylating agents like metronidazole and busulfan damage DNA directly rather than targeting a specific enzyme.

questions.stem: Which of these DNA sequence elements is the core promoter of a bacterial gene?

options.text: Transcription regulators bind it.
It codes for a protein or a functional RNA.
It makes the RNA polymerase fall off the gene.
The transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind it.

questions.answerRationale: The core promoter (including its -10 and -35 elements) is where RNA polymerase and its associated transcription/sigma factors bind to initiate transcription.

questions.stem: Which of these bacterial genes can be considered an operon?

options.text: It lacks regulatory elements.
It has core promoter elements at -10 and -35 regions.
It codes for a single protein or a single functional RNA.
It codes for more than one protein and/or functional RNAs.

questions.answerRationale: An operon is defined by its transcript coding for more than one protein and/or functional RNA under one promoter (polycistronic) - a single-product gene is not an operon regardless of its promoter or regulatory elements.

questions.stem: Which of these agents can be used to inhibit RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RDRP) of a virus?

options.text: Rifamycin.
Remdesivir.
Tetracycline.
Actinomycin D.

questions.answerRationale: Remdesivir is a nucleotide analog specifically designed to inhibit viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; the others target bacterial RNA polymerase, bacterial protein synthesis, or general transcription rather than a viral RDRP.

questions.stem: The nucleotide sequence of the top or coding strand of a bacterial gene is 5’AACCGGTT3’. What is the sequence of the RNA transcribed from the gene?

options.text: 5’AACCGGTT3’
5’AACCGGUU3’
5’TTGGCCAA3’
5’AACCGGTT3’ RNA grooming

questions.answerRationale: The coding (sense) strand has the same sequence as the mRNA except T is replaced by U, so 5'AACCGGTT3' transcribes to 5'AACCGGUU3'.

questions.stem: Which of the following methods of RNA grooming is defined INCORRECTLY?

options.text: RNA processing: removing useless portions of the pre-RNAs.
RNA splicing: Removing exons and sequentially ligating the introns.
RNA editing: Attaching nucleotides to an RNA after it is transcribed.
RNA modification: Chemically modifying nucleotide bases of an RNA after it is transcribed.

questions.answerRationale: Splicing removes introns and ligates the exons back together - this definition has it exactly backwards, describing the introns as kept and the exons as removed.

questions.stem: Which of the following bacterial RNAs are used by the cell without any grooming?

options.text: tRNA transcripts.
mRNA transcripts.
rRNA transcripts.
Any of these RNAs.

questions.answerRationale: Bacterial mRNA is typically used immediately after transcription with no processing (no capping, splicing, or poly-A tail, since bacteria generally lack introns), unlike tRNA and rRNA, which both require post-transcriptional processing before use.

sections.heading: Different types of RNAs and the fate of the RNA

questions.stem: Which of the following is a bacterial mRNA?

options.text: It has an RBSs, UTRs, and one or more ORFs
It is found in the 30S or 50S ribosomes.
It is foiled like the letter L
It carries an amino acid

questions.answerRationale: A bacterial mRNA is structurally defined by having a ribosome binding site, untranslated regions, and one or more open reading frames - the other options describe rRNA (ribosome component) or tRNA (L-shaped, carries an amino acid).

questions.stem: Challenge question: The nucleotide sequence of prokaryotic 16S rRNA is widely used to classify prokaryotes. Where does the 16S rRNA come from, and where can it be found?

options.text: They are transcribed from rRNA genes; they can be found in 50S ribosomes.
They are transcribed from rRNA genes, they can be found in 30S ribosomes.
They naturally occur as soluble RNAs in the cytoplasm of bacterial cells.

questions.answerRationale: 16S rRNA is transcribed from an rRNA gene and is a structural component of the small (30S) ribosomal subunit, not the large (50S) subunit or a free soluble cytoplasmic RNA.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a large subunit ribosome of a bacterial cell? See Fig. 5.21 of MMAHP to answer the question.

options.text: It contains 1 molecule of rRNA and 21 ribosomal proteins.
It contains 1 molecule of rRNA and 33 ribosomal proteins.
It contains 2 molecules of rRNA and 34 ribosomal proteins.
It contains 3 molecules of rRNA and 50 ribosomal proteins.

questions.answerRationale: The bacterial large (50S) ribosomal subunit contains two rRNA molecules (23S and 5S) plus roughly 31-34 ribosomal proteins - the small (30S) subunit is the one with a single rRNA (16S) and about 21 proteins.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a fully folded tRNA is CORRECT?

options.text: The amino acid is attached to its 5’ end.
Its anticodon is made of five nucleotides.
It folds to a cloverleaf (or cross-like) structure.
It contains an acceptor stem, a D loop, a T-psi-C loop, and an anticodon loop.

questions.answerRationale: A tRNA's named structural regions - the acceptor stem, D loop, T-psi-C loop, and anticodon loop - describe it correctly regardless of representation; "cloverleaf" is really the flattened secondary-structure diagram, while the tRNA's actual folded (tertiary) shape is L-shaped, not a cloverleaf.

questions.stem: Challenge question: The anticodon of a tRNA is 5’CCC3’. Which of the amino acids can an AATase use for charging the tRNA? Note: Please see Table 5.2 to answer the question.

options.text: Cys.
Ser.
Gly.
Ile.
Any of these.

questions.answerRationale: Anticodon 5'CCC3' pairs antiparallel with codon 5'GGG3', which codes for glycine.

questions.stem: The nucleotide sequence of an mRNA is 5’GCCAGGAUGCCCGGGAAAUUUCAGUGACCGAAA3’. What is the amino acid sequence of the protein its ORF encodes? Note: Please identify the ORF of the mRNA by finding the start codon AUG and the stop codon (which can be UAA, UAG, or UGA; then, use Table 5.2 to answer the question.

options.text: met-gly-lys-arg-pro-gly-ser
met-pro-gly-lys-phe-gln
ser-pro-gly-lys-leu-pro-gln
phe-gly-ala-leu-pro-gln-pro

questions.answerRationale: Reading from the AUG start codon (position 7) through UCC-GGG-AAA-UUU-CAG then the UGA stop codon gives Met-Pro-Gly-Lys-Phe-Gln.

questions.stem: Which of these amino acids has six codons? Note: Please use Table 5.2 to answer the question.

options.text: Val, Pro and Thr.
Leu, Ser and Arg.
Phe, Tyr and His.

questions.answerRationale: Leucine, serine, and arginine are each encoded by six different codons in the standard genetic code - the highest degree of degeneracy of any amino acids.

questions.stem: The Start codon is almost always_______ and the initator tRNA always carry the amino caid __________, thus, all newly syntheses proteins have that amino acid at its N terminus.

options.text: 5’UAA3’/Cys
5’UGA3’/His
5’UAA3’/Trp
5’AUG3’/ Met Protein synthesis

questions.answerRationale: AUG is almost always the start codon, and the initiator tRNA always carries methionine, which is why every newly synthesized protein begins with Met at its N-terminus (before any later trimming).

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally the first step of initiation of protein synthesis in a bacterial cell?

options.text: The small subunit ribosome binds an mRNA.
The small subunit ribosome binds a charged initiator tRNA.
The anticodon of the initiator tRNA aligns with the mRNA start codon.
The large subunit ribosome joins the small subunit ribosome and forms A, P, and E sites.

questions.answerRationale: Bacterial translation initiation begins with the small (30S) ribosomal subunit binding the mRNA at its ribosome binding site, before the charged initiator tRNA joins and the large subunit assembles the complete 70S ribosome.

questions.stem: The reaction of peptide bond formation between the amino acid of the A site tRNA and the amino acid or peptide chain of the P site tRNA is catalyzed by the enzyme activity (peptidyl transferase activity). Which of these is the peptidyl transferase activity a part of?

options.text: The uncharged tRNA.
The rRNAs in 50S ribosome subunit.
The rRNAs in 30S ribosome subunit.
Ribosomal proteins of the 30S and 50S ribosome subunits.

questions.answerRationale: Peptidyl transferase activity is a ribozyme function carried by the 23S rRNA within the large (50S) ribosomal subunit, not by any ribosomal protein or the small subunit.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT part of the translocation event of translation elongation?

options.text: The A site tRNA moves to the P site.
An amino acid enters the empty A site.
The A site of the 70S ribosome turns empty.
The 70S ribosome moves the mRNA by one codon.
The P-site tRNA becomes uncharged and moves to the E site.

questions.answerRationale: A new aminoacyl-tRNA entering the now-empty A site is the START of the NEXT elongation cycle, occurring after translocation is already complete - not part of the translocation step itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following can NOT be reused for protein synthesis immediately after translation termination?

options.text: The newly synthesized polypeptide chain
The 30S ribosomal subunit.
The 50S ribosomal subunit.
The mRNA.
The tRNAs.

questions.answerRationale: The finished polypeptide is the product of translation, released to fold and function on its own - unlike the ribosomal subunits, mRNA, and tRNAs, which are all machinery components immediately recycled for further rounds of protein synthesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of protein modification?

options.text: Part of a newly synthesized polypeptide chain is removed.
The newly synthesized polypeptide is acted on by a chaperonin.
The newly synthesized polypeptide is transported to its final destination.
Sugar or phosphate groups are attached to certain amino acids of the newly synthesized polypeptide.

questions.answerRationale: Attaching a sugar or phosphate group to specific amino acids after translation is literally the definition of post-translational protein modification, distinct from cleavage/processing, chaperone-assisted folding, or trafficking to a final destination.

questions.stem: Which of the following antibiotics inhibit RNA transcription by binding the 30S ribosome?

options.text: Rifamycin
Clindamycin.
Streptomycin.
Erythromycin.
Chloramphenicol.

questions.answerRationale: Streptomycin is the aminoglycoside that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks translation; rifamycin instead targets RNA polymerase directly, and the others bind the 50S subunit.

questions.stem: Which of the following antibiotics inhibit RNA transcription by binding the 50S ribosome?

options.text: Indinavir.
Quinolone.
Puromycin.
Tetracycline.
Metronidazole.

questions.answerRationale: Puromycin binds within the peptidyl transferase center of the 50S subunit, mimicking an aminoacyl-tRNA and causing premature chain termination - the others act elsewhere (RNA polymerase, DNA gyrase, DNA damage) or on the 30S subunit.

questions.stem: Which of these gives the genotype of a cell?

options.text: All the molecules found in the cell.
The nucleotide sequence of the genome of the cell.
All intact functional RNAs are found inside the cell.
All intact functional proteins are found inside the cell.

questions.answerRationale: A cell's genotype is its genetic makeup - the nucleotide sequence of its genome - as distinct from its expressed molecules (transcriptome/proteome), which reflect phenotype.

questions.stem: A bacterial cell has a protein named NtrC. It does not work until a PO4 group is attached to one of its aspartate residues. Is this protein a functional protein?

options.text: Yes, it is already available in the cell.
Yes, it is already synthesized.
No, it is not fully groomed.

questions.answerRationale: A protein that requires post-translational phosphorylation to become active is not yet "fully groomed" - the polypeptide has been synthesized, but it isn't functional until that modification is complete.

questions.stem: The cell can regulate gene expression at each of these steps. Which of them most accurately fine-tunes the regulatory measure?

options.text: Post-transcriptional (but pre-translational) level
Post-translational level
Pretranscription level
Transcriptional level
Translational level The lac operon and its regulation

questions.answerRationale: Post-translational regulation acts directly and immediately on already-made protein molecules (activating, inactivating, or modulating them), giving the fastest and most precisely graded control compared to regulation that only affects future rounds of transcription or translation.

questions.stem: Which of these can be called an enhancer for the expression of a lac operon?

options.text: lacZ, because it codes for beta-galactosidase, which acts on lactose.
The core promoter, because RNA polymerase and sigma factor bind it.
The CAP site, because CAP (a regulator) binds it and increases the rate of transcription.
Operator, because the lac repressor (a regulator) binds it and prevents RNA polymerase from binding the promoter.

questions.answerRationale: The CAP site is explicitly an activator element - CAP binding there increases the rate of transcription - unlike the operator (a silencer) or the core promoter (basal machinery binding site, not an enhancer).

questions.stem: Which of the proteins is the beta-galactosidase enzyme?

options.text: It can convert lactose to allolactose.
It can import lactose inside the cell.
It can modify/detoxify toxic sugars.
It is coed by the lacY orf the lac operon.

questions.answerRationale: Beta-galactosidase's well-known side activity, beyond hydrolyzing lactose, is isomerizing some lactose into allolactose - the molecule that actually inactivates the lac repressor; lactose import is lacY's (permease's) job, and beta-galactosidase is coded by lacZ, not lacY.

questions.stem: When E. coli grows on a medium having glucose but lacking lactose, which of the following must also take place?

options.text: cAMP is present in the cell.
Lac repressor binds to the operator.
The CAP protein is absent in the cell.
The cell has plenty of allolactose in the cytoplasm.

questions.answerRationale: With no lactose present, no allolactose can be made to inactivate it, so the lac repressor remains bound to the operator, keeping the operon off; glucose presence actually lowers cAMP levels rather than raising them, and CAP protein itself is always present in the cell regardless.

questions.stem: When allolactose is present in the cell, which of these events CANNOT take place?

options.text: The CAP binds cAMP and binds the CAP site (the enhancer).
The lac repressor binds the operator (silencer) of the lac operon.
The rate of transcription of the mRNA of the lac operon is at its highest.
The RNA polymerase-sigma factor binds the core promoter of the lac operon more frequently.

questions.answerRationale: Allolactose binds and inactivates the lac repressor, releasing it from the operator - so repressor-operator binding is exactly the event that cannot happen while allolactose is present.

questions.stem: Why does the CAP protein not bind the enhancer (i.e., CAP site) of the lac operon when the cell has glucose?

options.text: The cell lacks cAMP in that situation.
The cell lacks allolactose in that situation.
The cell lacks the CAP protein when glucose is present.
The lac repressor binds the CAP site when glucose is present.

questions.answerRationale: Glucose represses adenylate cyclase activity, keeping cAMP levels low - and CAP requires bound cAMP to activate and bind its site, so without cAMP, CAP cannot bind the enhancer regardless of how much CAP protein is present.

sections.heading: Part 1: Microbial Genetics Vertical vs horizontal (i.e., lateral) gene transfer

questions.stem: Gene transfer to offspring of sexual reproduction is ________ gene transfer, but the offspring of such organisms are genetically ____________ identical to each of the parent organisms.

options.text: horizontal/ almost 100%
vertical/ almost 100%
vertical/ about 50%
lateral/ about 50% Genetic and epigenetic variations

questions.answerRationale: Sexual reproduction passes genes from parent to offspring (vertical transfer), and each offspring gets half its genome from each parent - roughly 50% identical to either one, not nearly identical to both.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a mutation?

options.text: A cell gains a chunk of external DNA in one of its chromosomes.
Changes in the nucleotide sequences of a chromosome of a cell.
A diploid cell turns tetraploid.
A cell loses a chromosome.
All these.

questions.answerRationale: A mutation is any heritable change in genetic material - gaining inserted DNA, sequence changes, ploidy changes, and chromosome loss are all genuine forms of mutation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an epigenetic variation?

options.text: Methylation of the DNA of a gene in a genome.
Acetylation of histones of the chromatin of a genome.
Heritable phenotypic variations due to the methylation of DNA or the acetylation of histones of the chromatin.

questions.answerRationale: The DNA methylation or histone acetylation itself is just the molecular mechanism; "epigenetic variation" specifically refers to the resulting heritable phenotypic change caused by those modifications.

questions.stem: Mutations may cause each of the following problems EXCEPT__________.

options.text: eliminate the organism from the population
prevent DNA replication or gene transcription
alter the ability to control the expression of certain genes
prevent evolution through natural selection or other processes
prevent translation of an mRNA or change the function of a protein Point mutations

questions.answerRationale: Mutations are the raw material that fuels evolution by natural selection, not something that blocks it - the other four are all real, well-documented ways mutations can harm an organism.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a transversion type of point mutation?

options.text: Parental DNA 5’CCGGAA3’, daughter cell DNA 5’CCGTAA3’.
Parental DNA 5’CCGGAA3’, daughter cell DNA 5’CCGAAA3’.
Parental DNA 5’CCGGAA3’, daughter cell DNA 5’CCGGAAA3’.
Parental DNA 5’CCGGAA3’, daughter cell DNA 5’CCGAA3’.

questions.answerRationale: G->T (position 4, CCGGAA -> CCGTAA) swaps a purine for a pyrimidine, a transversion; G->A (option B) swaps purine for purine, a transition; options C and D are actually insertions/deletions, not substitutions at all.

questions.stem: Which of the following point mutations will cause a frame shift?

options.text: Transversion of a nucleotide in the ribosome binding site (RBS) region of a mRNA gene.
Insertion, deletion, or substitution mutations in the 3’ UTR region of a mRNA gene.
Insertion or deletion of one nucleotide inside the ORF of a mRNA gene.
Insertion, deletion, or substitution mutations in the spacer DNA.
Transition of one nucleotide in the ORF of a mRNA gene.

questions.answerRationale: A frameshift requires an insertion or deletion of nucleotides (not in multiples of three) within the coding region itself - substitutions, and indels outside the ORF, don't shift the reading frame.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements (about point mutations in the ORF of an mRNA gene) is a mismatch?

options.text: Silent mutation: The mutation has changed the codon but not the amino acid it codes.
Missense mutations: A mutation changed a codon and the amino acid it codes.
Frameshift mutation: Insertion or deletion of 1 or 2 nucleotides in the ORF.
Read-through mutation: The stop codon changed to a codon.
Nonsense mutations: A codon changed to an anticodon.

questions.answerRationale: A nonsense mutation converts a sense codon into a STOP codon - "changed to an anticodon" confuses an mRNA codon with an entirely separate tRNA structure and is not what nonsense mutations do.

questions.stem: Which of these defines polymorphism?

options.text: The mutation is rare (<1% of the population has it) and deleterious.
The mutation is common (>1% of the population has it) and neutral or beneficial.
It is a heritable variation stemming from the chemical modifications of DNA and histones.

questions.answerRationale: A polymorphism is, by definition, a genetic variant common in the population (over 1%) that is typically neutral or only mildly impactful - as opposed to a rare, deleterious mutation.

questions.stem: Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) is extremely common. If there is one SNP in every 1,000 bp of DNA, how many SNPs are present in the haploid genome of the human subject? Note: Human genome 3.2 billion bp.
questions.answerRationale: 3.2 billion bp / 1,000 bp per SNP = 3.2 million, roughly 3,000,000 SNPs.

questions.stem: Horses have 64 chromosomes, and donkeys have 62 chromosomes. What will be the karyotype of the mule sired by a horse and a donkey?

options.text: 62 chromosomes.
63 chromosomes.
64 chromosomes.
Depends on which species is the mother or father of the foal.

questions.answerRationale: Each parent contributes a haploid gamete: 32 chromosomes from the horse and 31 from the donkey, giving the mule 63 chromosomes total.

questions.stem: Which of these chromosomal anomalies is called translocation?

options.text: A segment of native DNA is removed from the chromosome.
A segment of non-native DNA is entered into the chromosome.
A portion of a chromosome moves to another location of the same chromosome.
A segment of a chromosome is replicated repeatedly and retained in the same chromosome.
A segment of DNA of the chromosome is inserted into the same location in reverse orientation.

questions.answerRationale: Among these options, a segment of a chromosome relocating elsewhere is the closest fit to translocation - as opposed to deletion (removing DNA), insertion of foreign DNA, duplication (repeated copies), or inversion (reversed orientation), which are each separately and correctly described by the other choices.

questions.stem: A DNA polymerase committed a nucleotide substitution mutation in one of the two strands of the dsDNA molecule. If not corrected, which of the following would suffer the consequences?

options.text: The mother cell.
Both daughter cells.
One of the two daughter cells.
The mother cell and both daughter cells.

questions.answerRationale: A single-strand substitution creates a heteroduplex; when the cell replicates, the correct strand templates a normal daughter while the erroneous strand templates a permanently mutated daughter - so only one of the two resulting daughter cells inherits the fixed mutation.

questions.stem: Which of the following would contribute to replication errors the most in an E. coli cell? Note: NTPs- ATP, CTP, etc.; dNTPs- dATP, dCTP, etc.

options.text: The cell contains more NTPs than dNTPs
The DNA polymerase lacks the proofreading function.
There are some DNA-binding agents, such as metronidazole, inside the cell.
The temperature of the surroundings is 25 degrees Celsius, not 37 degrees Celsius.

questions.answerRationale: Losing DNA polymerase's proofreading (3'-5' exonuclease) activity directly and dramatically increases the rate of uncorrected misincorporation errors, far more than the other listed factors.

sections.heading: Causes or mutations: Failure of the mismatch repair system

questions.stem: DNA mismatch repair system acts right after DNA replication to correct any non-(G-C) or non-(A-T) base pairs. How does the system correct the mismatch?

options.text: It removes and replaces the incorrect base with the correct base.
It removes the incorrect nucleotide with the correct nucleotide.
It removes a patch of ssDNA around the mismatched base pair, then DNA polymerase fills the gap.

questions.answerRationale: Mismatch repair excises a whole patch of single-stranded DNA around the mismatch (targeting the new, unmethylated strand) and lets DNA polymerase resynthesize the gap - it does not simply swap out one base or nucleotide in isolation.

questions.stem: Some DNA-damaging agents and damage mechanisms are listed below. Which of the statements is INCORRECT?

options.text: Methyl mercury: Donates the methyl group to nitrogenous bases (thus damaging DNA).
Gamma radiation: Ionizes water; the ions create reactive chemicals that break DNA.
Water: Removes adenine and guanine bases from nucleotides.
Water: removes the -NH2 group from A, G or C bases.
UV radiation: crosslinks G or A bases.

questions.answerRationale: UV radiation crosslinks adjacent PYRIMIDINE bases (forming thymine dimers, T-T or T-C), not purine bases like G or A - the other four statements about methyl mercury, gamma radiation, and water-driven depurination/deamination are all accurate.

questions.stem: Gamma radiation damages DNA by all these methods EXCEPT by ________.

options.text: cross-linking bases of DNA
ionizing water to create reactive ions
breaking the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA Repair of damaged DNA

questions.answerRationale: Gamma radiation acts by ionizing water into reactive radicals that break the DNA backbone - crosslinking adjacent bases is instead the signature mechanism of UV radiation.

questions.stem: Which of these bacterial enzymes removes crosslinking bonds between T-T and T-C bases of DNA?

options.text: UV photolyase.
Methyl transferases.
Base excision repair system.
Nucleotide excision repair system.

questions.answerRationale: UV photolyase directly reverses UV-induced pyrimidine dimers (T-T, T-C) using light energy - a direct, dedicated bond-breaking reversal, unlike nucleotide excision repair, which instead cuts out and replaces a whole patch around the lesion.

questions.stem: Base excision repair and nucleotide excision repair systems do some steps of the repair job and recruit additional enzymes to complete the job. Which of these do they make other enzymes to complete?

options.text: Detection of the damaged base or nucleotide.
Removal of the damaged base or nucleotide.
Removal of the base, or several nucleotides around the damaged nucleotide.
DNA synthesis to fill the gap (created by the removed nucleotides), and ligation of DNA.

questions.answerRationale: Base and nucleotide excision repair specialize in detecting and cutting out the damage, then hand off gap-filling and sealing to the cell's general-purpose DNA polymerase and DNA ligase.

questions.stem: Which of these types of DNA repair of broken DNA almost always adds mutations to the genome?

options.text: The SSBR system repairs ss DNA nicks.
The NHEJ system repairs dsDNA breaks.
The homologous recombination system repairs dsDNA breaks.

questions.answerRationale: Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repairs double-strand breaks by directly rejoining broken ends without a template, which is inherently error-prone and almost always introduces small insertions or deletions - unlike SSBR or homologous recombination, which both use an intact template strand for accurate repair.

sections.heading: Causes of mutations: Mobile DNA and biological mutagens

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT expected to happen after a bacterial DNA transposon moves?

options.text: Loss of a portion of a chromosome.
Loss of a gene function due to an insertion mutation.
Lateral transfer of the transposon to another bacterial cell.

questions.answerRationale: Transposition itself is a within-genome, within-cell event; moving a transposon does not by itself transfer it to another bacterial cell - that requires a separate mechanism like conjugation, transduction, or transformation.

questions.stem: Which of these can be considered a biological mutagen?

options.text: Transposons, DNA viruses, and viruses with cancer-causing genes (i.e., oncogenes).
Water, methyl mercury, methyl methane sulfonate, and potassium nitrite.
UV radiation, electron beam, and gamma radiation.
All these.

questions.answerRationale: Transposons and viruses (including oncogene-carrying ones) are biological entities and therefore biological mutagens - the other lists are chemical mutagens (water, methyl mercury, MMS, nitrite) and physical/radiation mutagens (UV, electron beam, gamma).

questions.stem: Which of the following viruses would mutate most readily?

options.text: A virus with a dsDNA genome.
A virus with an ssDNA genome.
A virus with an ssRNA genome.
A virus with a naked helical capsid.
A virus with an enveloped icosahedral capsid.

questions.answerRationale: RNA-dependent RNA polymerases generally lack proofreading activity, giving RNA viruses (especially ssRNA ones) far higher mutation rates than DNA viruses, whose polymerases do proofread; capsid structure has no bearing on mutation rate.

questions.stem: A porcine influenza virus infected a pig cell. Some progeny viruses had mutated genomes, affecting their hemagglutinin protein. Hemagglutinin is essential for the influenza virus to infect its host cell. Which of these will be the result of this mutation?

options.text: Antigenic drift.
Antigenic shift.
Antigenic drift or demise of the mutant virus.
Antigenic shift or demise of the mutant virus.

questions.answerRationale: Hemagglutinin mutations within a single infecting strain (no coinfection/reassortment involved) produce a small, gradual antigenic change (drift) if HA still functions, or kill off that mutant lineage entirely if the mutation breaks HA's essential function - "antigenic shift" requires segment reassortment between two co-infecting strains, which isn't the scenario described here. Note: the source PDF has a genuine typo, mislabeling two different options both "C" - the correct text is "Antigenic drift or demise of the mutant virus," not "Antigenic shift."

questions.stem: A person is infected simultaneously by human and avian influenza viruses. The influenza virus genome is composed of 8 different RNA molecules. Which of the following viruses generated in the cells of the person has undergone an antigenic shift?

options.text: The viruses that have all the human influenza virus genome fragments.
The viruses that have only the avian influenza virus genome fragments.
The viruses that have some human and some avian influenza virus genome fragments.

questions.answerRationale: Antigenic shift is defined by reassortment - a new virus assembled from a mix of gene segments from both co-infecting strains, not one made purely of either parent's segments alone.

sections.heading: Fate of foreign DNA entering bacterial cells

questions.stem: A linear piece of dsDNA was introduced into a bacterial cell. The nucleotide sequence of the incoming DNA is NOT at all similar to the nucleotide sequences in the cell's genome. The incoming DNA lacks a replication origin. Which of these outcomes is NOT expected of this event?

options.text: The dsDNA molecule will be destroyed by the cell’s nucleases.
The dsDNA would be randomly inserted into the cell's chromosomes.
One of the two strands of the incoming dsDNA would be recombined into the cell’s chromosome.

questions.answerRationale: Homologous recombination absolutely requires sequence similarity to align and exchange strands, which this incoming DNA explicitly lacks - so that outcome, unlike nuclease destruction or rare non-homologous insertion, is essentially impossible here.

questions.stem: A linear piece of dsDNA was inserted into a bacterial cell. The nucleotide sequence of the inserted DNA is quite similar to that in the cell's genome. The incoming DNA lacks a replication origin. Which of these outcomes is the most likely outcome of this event?

options.text: The inserted DNA would be entirely destroyed by the cells’ nucleases.
The inserted DNA would replicate and be distributed to the daughter cells.
One of the two strands of the inserted dsDNA would be recombined into the cell’s chromosome.

questions.answerRationale: With genuine sequence similarity now present, homologous recombination becomes the most likely fate: one strand of the incoming DNA can be recombined directly into the matching region of the host chromosome.

questions.stem: Which of these is gene conversion?

options.text: Variation due to mismatch repair of the heteroduplex formed in a homologous recombination event.
When a mutant/nonfunctional gene turns into a functional gene.
When a functional gene turns a mutant/nonfunctional gene.

questions.answerRationale: Gene conversion is specifically the outcome of mismatch repair acting on the heteroduplex DNA formed during homologous recombination, non-reciprocally converting one sequence to match the other - not simply any mutation toward or away from function.

sections.heading: Lateral DNA transfer: Transfection and bacterial transformation

questions.stem: A eukaryotic cell is transformed if it __________, a bacterial cell is transformed if it ________.

options.text: becomes a tumor cell/ receives foreign DNA
receives foreign DNA/ becomes a mutant cell
have mutations of any type/ have mutations of any type

questions.answerRationale: In eukaryotic cell biology "transformation" specifically means becoming a tumor cell, a completely different, unrelated usage from the bacterial term, where "transformation" means taking up foreign DNA from the environment.

questions.stem: Prokaryotic cells that have suffered DNA damage become naturally competent. What can a naturally competent cell do that an ordinary bacterial cell can’t?

options.text: They die from programmed cell death.
They aggressively destroy DNA inserted into them.
They may actively collect and internalize DNA from the environment.

questions.answerRationale: Natural competence is defined by the ability to actively take up and internalize extracellular DNA - the opposite of aggressively destroying incoming DNA, which an ordinary (non-competent) cell already does by default.

questions.stem: Which of the following DNA molecules can a competent bacterium pick up and internalize?

options.text: Pure DNA extracted from bacterial cells and dissolved in distilled water.
DNA released by a dead bacterium in the fecal materials of the colon.
DNA was released by a dead archaeon in the mud of a tidal pond.
Viral or plasmid DNA.
Any of these.

questions.answerRationale: Natural competence machinery takes up extracellular DNA fairly indiscriminately regardless of its species of origin or whether it's chromosomal, plasmid, or viral - as long as it's accessible DNA in the environment.

questions.stem: Someone wants to insert a human gene into E. coli cells. Which of the following processes will be least helpful in achieving her goal?

options.text: Pack human DNA in a lipid vesicle and mix it with the bacterial cell.
Mix human DNA and the cells and momentarily pulse the mixture with a high electric voltage.
Add human DNA to a solution containing anions (such as SO4-2 ions) and mix it with bacterial cells.
Add human DNA to a solution containing some cations (such as Ca+2) and mix it with bacterial cells.
Mix human DNA and the cells and momentarily treat the mixture with high temperature (i.e. 42o C for 30 sec).

questions.answerRationale: Standard bacterial transformation relies on CATIONS (like Ca2+) to neutralize the charge repulsion between DNA's negative phosphate backbone and the negatively charged bacterial membrane; using anions instead would not help and works against the mechanism that makes lipofection, electroporation, CaCl2/heat-shock, and heat shock alone all genuinely effective.

questions.stem: Which of the following phages would be most suitable for treating multidrug-resistant bacterial infections?

options.text: A phage that can cause lytic infection but not lysogenic infection.
A phage that can cause lysogenic infection but not lytic infection.
A phage that can cause both lysogenic and lytic infections.
A phage that was isolated from a sewage sample.

questions.answerRationale: A purely lytic phage always kills its bacterial host without any risk of dormant lysogeny (which could confer resistance to further phage treatment), making it the most reliable, predictable choice for phage therapy.

questions.stem: Which of the following phages is NOT a defective phage? Note: A defective phage particle may infect a bacterium and inject its DNA into the bacterium, but it would not be able to cause a lytic or lysogenic infection.

options.text: The phage particle contains a phage genome that is attached to a fragment of bacterial DNA.
The phage particle contains a fragment of bacterial DNA, not a phage genome.
The phage has its own genome, free of mutations.

questions.answerRationale: A phage genome that is fully intact and mutation-free is, by definition, a normal functional phage - not defective at all, unlike particles carrying no phage genome or only a fragment attached to bacterial DNA.

questions.stem: Which of the following phages may cause specialized transduction?

options.text: Progeny phages generated from a lytic infection.
Progeny of a (lysogenic) prophage carrying only its own genome.
Progeny of a (isogenic) prophage carrying a portion of host chromosomal DNA.

questions.answerRationale: Specialized transduction happens when a prophage excises imprecisely from a specific chromosomal location, dragging an adjacent piece of host DNA along with its own genome into the next host it infects.

questions.stem: Which of the following plasmids will allow the host bacterium to become resistant to the antibiotic neomycin?

options.text: F fator plasmids.
R factor plasmids.
Diissimilation (D) plasmids.
Bacteriocinogenic plasmids.

questions.answerRationale: R (resistance) factor plasmids are specifically defined by carrying antibiotic resistance genes, unlike F (fertility), dissimilation, or bacteriocinogenic plasmids, which serve entirely different functions.

questions.stem: Which of these must a plasmid have to survive and perpetuate in a host bacterium?

options.text: A replication origin.
A circular dsDNA genome.
A gene for the pilus protein.
A gene for an antibiotic resistance enzyme.
A gene that codes for a peptide antibiotic (such as colicin).

questions.answerRationale: A functional replication origin is the one absolute requirement for a plasmid to be copied and passed on by the host's replication machinery - none of the other listed genes or the exact genome shape are universally necessary.

questions.stem: A Gram-negative bacterium is resistant to ampicillin because of having an F factor plasmid carrying an Amp- resistant gene. Can a Gram-positive bacterium living in the same environment get the plasmid?

options.text: Yes, via conjugation only.
Yes, via transformation only.
Yes, via conjugation or transformation.
No, the bacteria are phylogenetically unrelated.

questions.answerRationale: Standard F-factor-mediated conjugation pili are not compatible with Gram-positive cell envelopes, so conjugation across the Gram divide is not viable this way - but a naturally competent Gram-positive cell could still take up free plasmid DNA released into the environment via transformation, regardless of the donor's Gram status.

questions.stem: Which of these is an F’ bacterium?

options.text: It has an F factor plasmid.
It lacks an F factor plasmid.
It has an F factor plasmid integrated into its chromosome.
It has a free F factor plasmid to which a piece of chromosomal DNA is ligated.

questions.answerRationale: An F' bacterium is defined by having a free F factor plasmid to which a piece of chromosomal DNA has been ligated, following imprecise excision from an Hfr chromosome - distinct from F+ (free F factor alone), F- (no F factor), or Hfr (F factor still integrated).

questions.stem: An F- bacterium may receive part of the chromosomal DNA from which of these bacterial strains?

options.text: hfr.
F+ or F’.
F’ or hfr.

questions.answerRationale: Both F' and Hfr donors transfer part of the host chromosome along with (or instead of) the plasmid itself during conjugation, unlike plain F+ strains, which normally transfer only the free F plasmid.

questions.stem: Is bacterial conjugation a form of sexual reproduction?

options.text: Yes, because F+ cells conjugate with F- cells.
Yes, because the process involves gene transfer.
No, because the cells do not fuse to make a zygote.
No, because the DNA transfer is one-way, not mutual.

questions.answerRationale: True sexual reproduction requires two gametes to physically fuse into a zygote combining both genomes; bacterial conjugation involves no cell fusion or zygote formation at all.

questions.stem: A bacterium received DNA from another bacterium via transformation, transduction, or conjugation. What will happen to the DNA in the recipient cell?

options.text: The cell will destroy the DNA using nucleases.
The DNA will perpetuate in the cell as free DNA and pass to its progeny.
The cell will use the DNA for homologous recombination/gene conversion.
The cell will have the DNA randomly inserted into one of its chromosomes.
Any of these outcomes is possible, based on the information on the incoming DNA.

questions.answerRationale: The actual fate of incoming DNA - degraded, recombined, randomly inserted, or persisting as free replicating DNA - genuinely depends on properties of that specific DNA, like whether it shares sequence homology with the host genome or carries its own origin of replication.

questions.stem: Which of the following defines or describes genetic engineering?

options.text: Making cheese using cow’s milk and Lactobacillus bulgaricus.
PCR-cloning a growth hormone gene using bovine cDNA.
Producing human growth factor (protein) in bacteria.
Ligating two molecules of DNA in a test tube.

questions.answerRationale: Deliberately isolating and copying a specific gene using targeted molecular techniques (PCR-cloning from cDNA) is a direct act of genetic engineering, unlike traditional fermentation (no DNA manipulation) or simply using an already-engineered organism to make a protein.

questions.stem: Cellular DNA is extracted by breaking open the cell wall, destroying the lipid membranes, and denaturing proteins and RNA. Which of the following agents destroys the cell wall?

options.text: Proteinase K or other proteases.
Lysozyme or lyticase.
Phenol or chloroform.
Chelators such as EDTA.
Detergents such as SDS.

questions.answerRationale: Lysozyme and lyticase are enzymes that specifically degrade bacterial and fungal cell walls (peptidoglycan and chitin/glucan, respectively) - the other agents target proteins, membranes, or nucleic acid stability instead.

questions.stem: All these can be used in DNA extraction EXCEPT _______, which is usually used in extracting RNA.

options.text: salt such as potassium chloride
guanidium isothiocyanate
detergents such as SDS
enzymes such as RNases
chelators such as EDTA cDNA synthesis

questions.answerRationale: Guanidinium isothiocyanate is the classic reagent associated with RNA extraction protocols (denaturing RNases while preserving RNA); the other agents (salts, SDS, RNases to remove contaminating RNA, and EDTA) are all standard tools of DNA extraction.

questions.stem: Which of these is not necessary for cDNA synthesis?

options.text: An RNA template (mRNA, rRNA, tRNA, or synthetic RNA).
NTPs (i.e., ATP, CTP, UTP, and GTP).
Reverse transcriptase (an enzyme).
A primer DNA.

questions.answerRationale: Reverse transcriptase builds a DNA strand from an RNA template, so it needs dNTPs (DNA building blocks), a primer, and the RNA itself - not NTPs, which are the building blocks for RNA, not DNA.

questions.stem: Which of these is a peptide synthesizer?

options.text: It uses amino acids as the raw ingredients.
It uses dNTPs as the raw ingredients.
It uses NTPs as the raw ingredients.

questions.answerRationale: A peptide synthesizer chemically links amino acids together to build a peptide chain, so amino acids are its raw ingredients - dNTPs and NTPs are instead the building blocks of DNA and RNA synthesizers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a clone?

options.text: Copies of PCR-amplified DNA produced by two unique primers.
Chicks hatched from unfertilized eggs of a female turkey.
Chicks hatched from fertilized eggs of a female turkey.
Daughter cells and granddaughter cells of a bacterium.

questions.answerRationale: Fertilized eggs combine genetic material from two parents, producing a genetically unique individual - not a clone of either parent, unlike PCR copies, parthenogenetic (unfertilized-egg) offspring, or bacterial daughter cells, all of which are genetically identical (clonal) to their source.

questions.stem: Which of the following steps of a PCR is CORRECTLY described?

options.text: 55 degrees C: The DNA polymerase extends the primers.
72 degrees C: Allows the primers to anneal to ssDNA.
95 degrees C: Denatures dsDNA to ssDNA.

questions.answerRationale: Standard PCR cycling runs ~95°C to denature dsDNA into single strands, ~50-60°C to anneal primers, and ~72°C for polymerase extension - the other two options swap the annealing and extension temperatures' roles.

questions.stem: How is RT-PCR different from conventional PCR?

options.text: RT-PCR uses reverse transcriptase to copy DNA; PCR uses DNA polymerase to do the same.
RT-PCR uses cDNA as the template; PCR uses DNA as the template.
RT-PCR uses NTPs to copy DNA; PCR uses dNTPs to do the same.
RT-PCR does not use primers; PCR does.

questions.answerRationale: RT-PCR starts by reverse-transcribing RNA into cDNA, which then serves as the amplification template - a DNA-form template derived from RNA, as opposed to conventional PCR working directly from genomic DNA; RT-PCR still uses primers and dNTPs like standard PCR.

questions.stem: Which of these is necessary for detecting HPV, a DNA virus (extracted from human skin cells) by PCR?

options.text: The virus DNA must be separated from contaminating human DNA and RNA.
The primers should anneal to the viral DNA, not to any other DNA.
The virus must have a linear DNA genome.

questions.answerRationale: PCR specificity comes from primer design - primers that anneal only to the viral sequence will amplify just that target even in a background of overwhelming excess human DNA, with no need to physically separate the templates beforehand.

sections.heading: Vectored cloning: Cloning vectors, DNA ligation, and transfection

questions.stem: Which of the following features must a cloning vector have for it to be able to replicate inside the transfected cell?

options.text: It should contain a multicloning site (MCS) with suitable restriction endonuclease digestion sites.
It should contain marker or reporter genes, such as the ampicillin resistance gene.
It should be a circular dsDNA molecule.
It should contain a replication origin.

questions.answerRationale: Without a replication origin recognized by the host cell's machinery, a vector simply cannot be copied, regardless of what other features (multicloning site, marker genes, circularity) it carries.

questions.stem: In which aspect is vectored cloning superior to PCR cloning?

options.text: Time it takes to finish cloning.
The size of DNA that can be cloned.
Amounts of cloned DNA that can be generated.
Ease of isolating the DNA fragments to be cloned.

questions.answerRationale: Vectors like BACs and YACs can carry and stably replicate much larger DNA inserts than PCR can reliably amplify, which is the clear advantage of vectored cloning over PCR-based cloning; PCR is actually faster and yields more DNA per reaction.

questions.stem: The steps of vectored cloning are listed below. Which of these is the third step (from start to finish) of the process?

options.text: Transfect competent E. coli cells using the ligated DNA.
Mix the prepared vector and the insert DNA and add DNA ligase.
Prepare the cloning vector by digesting with the appropriate restriction endonuclease.
Isolate the insert DNA to be cloned; cut it with the appropriate restriction endonuclease.

questions.answerRationale: Vectored cloning runs: isolate and cut the insert, prepare (cut) the vector, mix the two and add ligase, then transfect competent cells with the ligated product - making the ligation step third.

questions.stem: Which of the following methods of transfection is most suitable for plant cells (in tissue culture)?

options.text: Brief electric shock (also called electroporation).
Brief heat shock (i.e., heat-shock-poration).
Lipid micelles (also called lipofection).
Microinjection.
Gene gun.

questions.answerRationale: The gene gun (biolistic delivery) physically shoots DNA-coated particles through a plant cell's rigid cell wall, the one barrier that makes electroporation, lipofection, or microinjection alone poorly suited to walled plant cells.

sections.heading: Use of Cloned DNA: Modern DNA sequencing

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT necessary for sequencing DNA if DNA polymerase is used for the purpose?

options.text: Sensors to detect which nucleotide was used for DNA synthesis.
Computer software to record and report the nucleotide sequence.
The four nucleotides; each labeled with a different fluorescent dye.
Template DNA (i.e., ssDNA) to be sequenced and a short DNA primer.
A ring-shaped protein (nanopore) through which ssDNA would travel.

questions.answerRationale: A ring-shaped nanopore protein belongs to an entirely different sequencing technology (nanopore sequencing, which reads DNA electrically as it threads through the pore) that does not use DNA polymerase at all - unlike sensors, software, fluorescent nucleotides, and a template/primer, which are all genuinely needed for polymerase-based (e.g. Sanger-style) sequencing.

questions.stem: The steps of Shotgun genome sequencing are listed below. Which of them is step 2 from the beginning?

options.text: Isolate the bacterium to a pure culture.
Clone the DNA fragments using a plasmid cloning vector.
Sequence the cloned DNA fragment and get its nucleotide sequence.
Extract DNA and fragment it by cutting with a restriction endonuclease.
Use a computer to align the nucleotide sequences to get the full genome sequence.

questions.answerRationale: Shotgun sequencing runs: isolate a pure culture, extract and fragment the DNA with a restriction enzyme, clone the fragments into a plasmid vector, sequence each clone, then computationally align all the reads - making DNA extraction/fragmentation the second step.

sections.heading: Use of cloned DNA: DNA fingerprinting

questions.stem: Which of these allows DNA fingerprinting by restriction fragment-length polymorphism (RFLP) to identify different individuals of the same species?

options.text: Random mutation in the genome of different individuals of the same species.
The difference in the size of the genomes of different individuals of the same species.
Random mutations in the genome that affect some restriction endonuclease digestion sites.

questions.answerRationale: RFLP fingerprinting works because individual-to-individual mutations create or destroy specific restriction enzyme recognition sites, producing different-sized DNA fragments after digestion - not because of any difference in overall genome size.

sections.heading: Use of cloned DNA: Transgenesis, DNA vaccine, and edible vaccines

questions.stem: Which of the following is a transgenic organism and a GMO or LMO?

options.text: A twig of a Gala apple tree grafted to the stem of a crabapple tree.
A mule born to a mare mother and a donkey father.
A baby born to an artificially inseminated woman.
A rice plant carrying a gene from a carrot plant.

questions.answerRationale: A rice plant carrying a gene transferred in from an unrelated species (a carrot) via genetic engineering is the definition of transgenic/GMO - grafting, natural interspecies hybridization (mule), and assisted human reproduction all involve no laboratory genetic modification at all.

questions.stem: Edible vaccines are vaccines integrated into food substances. Which of these serves as the true vaccine in an edible vaccine?

options.text: The glycoprotein gene of a pathogenic virus inserted into the chromosome of a strawberry plant.
Strawberries of a plant transgenic for the viral glycoprotein gene.
Viral glycoprotein expressed in the strawberries.
The glycoprotein gene of a pathogenic virus.

questions.answerRationale: The actual immunogenic component - the viral glycoprotein protein itself, expressed and present in the edible tissue - is what triggers an immune response when eaten; the inserted gene and the transgenic plant/fruit are just the means of producing that antigen.

questions.stem: Why are DNA vaccines not administered in humans?

options.text: DNA may be inserted into the human genome, leading to harmful mutations.
All needed vaccines for human diseases are available in traditional form.
DNA vaccines work only in animals, not in human cells.
DNA vaccination is excessively painful.

questions.answerRationale: The standard cited safety concern is that DNA vaccines could integrate into the human genome and cause harmful mutations - not that alternatives already exist, that they don't work in humans, or that administration is unusually painful.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the definition of bioinformatics?

options.text: Sequencing genomes of microorganisms.
Identifying the mRNAs expressed by a tumor cell.
Application of computers to the interpretation of biological data.

questions.answerRationale: Bioinformatics is generally defined as the application of computers to interpreting biological data - genome sequencing and specific analyses like tumor mRNA profiling are applications of the field, not its definition.

questions.stem: You want to find out the nucleotide sequence of an mRNA of a gene of Helicobacter pylori. Which of the following databases should you investigate?

options.text: TIGR.
PubMed.
GenBank.
Swissprot.

questions.answerRationale: GenBank is the primary nucleotide sequence database for looking up a gene's mRNA/DNA sequence; PubMed indexes literature, Swissprot is a protein sequence database, and TIGR was a genome sequencing institute rather than a general lookup database.

questions.stem: Which of the following ethical problems regarding biotechnology is far-fetched as of today?

options.text: Unforeseen effects of gene therapy.
Manipulation of the germline human genome.
Leakage or trading of personal genetic information.
Restoration of extinct species through cloning and hybridization.
Severe food allergy and inflammatory bowel disease from GM food crops.

questions.answerRationale: Restoring extinct species through cloning remains a largely theoretical, unrealized prospect - no extinct species has actually been restored to date - unlike gene therapy risk, germline editing, genetic privacy, and GM food safety concerns, which are all live, ongoing real-world debates today.

questions.stem: Which of the following suspicions on GM/LM organisms have been found to be a significant proven reality as of today?

options.text: Dissemination of GMO super pests in nature.
Dissemination of GMO superweeds in nature.
Fatal health effects of GMO grains and vegetables.
Market monopoly and market manipulation by biotech companies.

questions.answerRationale: Herbicide-resistant "superweeds" (like glyphosate-resistant Palmer amaranth) evolving and spreading due to widespread herbicide-tolerant GM crop use is a well-documented, proven reality - unlike claims of fatal GM food health effects, which have not been substantiated despite extensive study.

chapters.title: How to Grow and Control Microbial Growth

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences best expresses the reality of the growth of a unicellular microbe?

options.text: A daughter bacterial cell becomes as large as the mother cell.
A thousand bacteria are generated from a single bacterium.
A bacterium produced an endospore.

questions.answerRationale: For a unicellular microbe, "growth" specifically means an increase in cell NUMBER through repeated division, not an individual cell growing larger (which just restores it to normal size after division) or forming a dormant endospore.

sections.heading: How microbes grow in the natural environment

questions.stem: All microbes are essentially __________ organisms because __________.

options.text: terrestrial/microbes may grow on semisolid media
aquatic/ about 70% of the volume of cytoplasm is water
terrestrial/microbial envelope is designed to resist desiccation
aquatic/microbes have few adaptations to live in dry environments

questions.answerRationale: Every cell, regardless of habitat, is fundamentally an aquatic system - roughly 70% of cytoplasm by volume is water, and all of a cell's biochemistry happens in that aqueous environment.

questions.stem: Which of the following may not harm microbial growth in natural environments?

options.text: Acid rain or alkaline factory runoff.
Water completely fills the air capillaries of the soil.
Excessive microbial species diversity in one environment.
Presence of excess heavy metals and synthetic chemicals in the soil.

questions.answerRationale: High species diversity is a sign of a healthy, resource-rich environment, not a stressor - unlike acid/alkaline pollution, waterlogged (anaerobic) soil, or heavy metal/chemical contamination, which are all genuine growth-harming factors.

questions.stem: Although there are millions of bacterial species, only about 6,000 have been identified and named so far. Which of the following is the most plausible reason?

options.text: Most bacteria that live in the environment are inaccessible to microbiologists.
Most bacteria are harmless and thus not interesting to microbiologists.
Most bacterial species cannot be grown in the laboratory media.
Most bacteria live inside the cells of other organisms.

questions.answerRationale: This is the well-known "great plate count anomaly" - most environmental bacterial species have never been successfully cultured on standard laboratory media.

questions.stem: Which of the following bacterial infections will be most difficult to treat?

options.text: Bacteria growing in the blood.
Bacteria growing on the mucous membrane.
Bacteria growing inside the lung, forming a biofilm.

questions.answerRationale: Biofilm-forming bacteria deep in the lung are notoriously hard to treat because the biofilm matrix blocks antibiotic penetration and shelters resistant "persister" cells - unlike bacteria freely circulating in blood or sitting on an exposed mucous membrane.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most suitable substratum for pathogenic bacteria (in the human body) to form a biofilm?

options.text: An IUD or a pacemaker.
The inner wall of a vein or an artery.
The surfaces of the heart and the heart valves.
The surface of the trachea, bronchioles, or alveoli.

questions.answerRationale: Inert, non-living, foreign surfaces like an IUD or pacemaker are the classic, textbook-favorite substrate for pathogenic biofilm formation, since they lack the active blood flow and immune surveillance that would otherwise disrupt biofilm establishment on living tissue.

questions.stem: Which of these may contain viral pathogens that can cause respiratory infections?

options.text: Conditioned air coming out from room ducts.
Air released by cooling tower of an electric plant.
Air of a office room where five people are sit for six hours.
Air released by a modern incinerator for burning solid waste including animal carcass.

questions.answerRationale: Respiratory droplets exhaled by people sharing an enclosed space for hours is the classic route for airborne viral transmission - filtered/conditioned air, cooling-tower aerosols (a bacterial/Legionella concern), and incinerator exhaust are not typical viral transmission vehicles.

questions.stem: Optimum growth temperatures of some microbes are shown below. Which of the microbes is a psychrotroph?

options.text: 15 degrees C.
25 degrees C.
37 degrees C.
52 degrees C.
72 degrees C.

questions.answerRationale: Psychrotrophs tolerate cold storage temperatures but still grow best in a moderate, mesophile-like range (around 20-30°C) rather than at true cold-loving (psychrophile) optimum temperatures.

questions.stem: The range and optimum temperatures for growth of mesophiles are _________, respectively.

options.text: 0-30 degrees C and 25 degrees C
10-50 degrees C and 30 degrees C
30-65 degrees C and 50 degrees C
15-42 degrees C and 37 degrees C

questions.answerRationale: The standard mesophile range and optimum (roughly 15-42°C, optimum ~37°C) matches human-body-temperature-adapted organisms; the other ranges describe cooler or more thermophilic microbes.

questions.stem: Which of the following solutions will cause a bacterium (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) to suffer plasmolysis?

options.text: Seawater (contains 3.5% salt).
Freshwater (contains <0.05% salt).
Blood plasma (295 milliosmole/kg).
Normal saline solution (contains 0.9% salt).

questions.answerRationale: Seawater at 3.5% salt is strongly hypertonic relative to bacterial cytoplasm, drawing water out and causing plasmolysis; freshwater is hypotonic (causes swelling), and blood plasma and normal saline are roughly isotonic to the cell.

questions.stem: An obligate anaerobe such as Clostridium perfringens must ________ to survive in the bottom mud of a pond.

options.text: remove free radicals and detoxify reactive oxygen species
ferment or conduct anaerobic respiration to obtain ATP
form endospores
produce biofilm Chemical and biological factors of microbial growth

questions.answerRationale: As an obligate anaerobe, this organism cannot use oxidative phosphorylation at all, so its only way to generate ATP in the anoxic mud is fermentation or anaerobic respiration using a non-oxygen terminal electron acceptor.

questions.stem: Why do aerobes need enzymes such as SOD, catalase, and oxidase?

options.text: To convert CO2 to O2.
To convert O2 to CO2.
To detoxify reactive oxygen species (ROS).
To harvest oxygen and to increase the rate of respiration.

questions.answerRationale: SOD, catalase, and related enzymes exist specifically to detoxify the reactive oxygen species generated as byproducts of aerobic metabolism - they don't convert CO2/O2 into each other or directly boost respiration rate.

questions.stem: Which of the following chemical reactions does the enzyme SOD catalyze?

options.text: H2O2 + NADH + H+ ® 2H2O +NAD+

questions.answerRationale: This is literally the superoxide dismutase reaction: 2O2- + 2H+ -> H2O2 + O2, converting toxic superoxide into less-reactive hydrogen peroxide and oxygen.

questions.stem: A bacterium uses oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, but lacks SOD and peroxidase. The bacterium is most likely a ________.

options.text: microaerophile
obligatory aerobe
obligate anaerobe
facultative anaerobe
aerotolerant anaerobe
