questions.answerRationale: An organism that uses oxygen but has limited antioxidant defenses (rather than none at all, which would be fatal for any oxygen-using cell) fits a microaerophile - one that needs oxygen but only tolerates it at reduced concentrations because it can't fully detoxify the ROS produced at full atmospheric levels.

questions.stem: All the following are reactive oxygen species (ROS). Which of them is the singlet oxygen?

options.text: O3
OH.
H2O2

questions.answerRationale: "1O2" is the standard chemical notation for singlet oxygen, an excited-state form of molecular oxygen - distinct from superoxide (O2-), ozone (O3), the hydroxyl radical (OH·), and hydrogen peroxide.

questions.stem: Which of the following bacteria, by definition, is an obligate halophile?

options.text: It does not grow in the presence of NaCl.
It needs NaCl in the medium to grow.
It tolerates a low concentration of NaCl but not a high concentration of NaCl.

questions.answerRationale: An obligate halophile is defined by requiring salt in the medium to grow at all - the opposite of an organism that can't tolerate salt, or one with only limited salt tolerance.

questions.stem: Some sulfur bacteria survive in acid pools near copper mines. These bacteria are _________, and their enzymes must function well at the pH_______.

options.text: acidophile/ 2-4
acidophile/ 6-7
alkaliphile/8-10

questions.answerRationale: Acidophilic sulfur bacteria near copper mines thrive at pH 2-4, an environment their enzymes are specifically adapted to function well in.

questions.stem: The main sources of nutrients of pathogenic bacteria (living in the human body) are shown below. One of the sources is incorrect. The item is ___________.

options.text: carbon: Organic molecules from live or dead cells
nitrogen: N2 gas and dissolved nitrate salts
phosphorus: nucleic acids
trace elements: water
sulfur: amino acids Aseptic techniques and growth media

questions.answerRationale: Pathogenic bacteria living in the human body get nitrogen from organic host sources like amino acids and proteins, not from fixing atmospheric N2 gas or reducing nitrate salts - those are capabilities of specialized environmental/soil bacteria, not typical human pathogens.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the routine laboratory septic techniques?

options.text: Keep culture media sterile.
Protect laboratory workers from infections.
Dispose of the biohazard wastes in a septic tank.
Prevent contamination of the microbial culture media.

questions.answerRationale: A septic tank is a wastewater treatment system for untreated sewage, not an approved method for disposing of biohazardous laboratory waste, which requires autoclaving, incineration, or dedicated biohazard disposal - a serious protocol breach, not a routine aseptic technique.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of the semisolid culture media?

options.text: The media is formed in plates or tubes.
Can be scaled up to grow a large batch of microbes.
Many but not all microbes grow on semisolid media.
Establishing a pure culture or growing microbes that need a substratum.

questions.answerRationale: Semisolid media sit between liquid and fully rigid solid media, making them useful for isolating pure cultures or growing organisms that need some physical substratum without requiring a fully solid surface.

questions.stem: A medium has water, glucose, NaCl, MgSO4, K2HPO4, KH2PO4, agar, and tap water. The medium is a ________ medium.

options.text: defined broth
defined semisolid
complex semisolid
selective semisolid

questions.answerRationale: Every ingredient listed (glucose, specific salts, buffers) is a known, pure chemical compound, making this a chemically DEFINED medium, and the presence of agar makes it semisolid.

questions.stem: In MacConkey agar plates, G(+) bacteria, G(-) non-enteric bacteria do not grow but G(-) enteric bacteria grow with different colony characteristics. The medium is a ________.

options.text: selective medium
differential medium
enrichment medium
selective-differential medium Growing bacteria and bacterial growth curve

questions.answerRationale: MacConkey agar both SELECTS for Gram-negative enteric bacteria (inhibiting Gram-positives and non-enteric Gram-negatives) AND DIFFERENTIATES among the enterics that do grow by their distinct colony characteristics - doing both jobs simultaneously.

questions.stem: Capnophile bacteria needs an environment with ___________ to grow.

options.text: low oxygen and high nitrogen concentration
higher CO2 and lower oxygen level
high moisture

questions.answerRationale: Capnophiles specifically require an atmosphere enriched in CO2 and reduced in oxygen to grow, unlike organisms that just need low oxygen or high humidity alone.

questions.stem: Which of these is inappropriate for growing obligate anaerobes?

options.text: Plates incubated in a candle jar.
Medium contains sodium thioglycolate.
Plates incubated in an oxygen-free/nitrogen-rich atmosphere.

questions.answerRationale: A candle jar only depletes oxygen partially (until the candle self-extinguishes), leaving several percent O2 behind - fine for capnophiles/microaerophiles but insufficient for true obligate anaerobes, unlike a genuinely oxygen-free atmosphere or an oxygen-scavenging reducing agent like sodium thioglycolate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the stationary phase of a bacterial growth curve?

options.text: In this phase, the death rate is high, and the growth rate is low.
In this phase, the death and growth rates are nearly identical.
In this phase, the death rate is negligible, the growth rate is fixed and high.
In this phase, the death rate is negligible, and the growth rate is negligible or very low.

questions.answerRationale: The stationary phase is defined by the death rate and growth rate becoming nearly equal, holding the population roughly constant - unlike log phase (high growth, low death) or decline phase (death dominates).

questions.stem: One should harvest bacterial cells at the _______ phase to isolate biologically active enzymes, and ________ phase to extract antibiotics.

options.text: lag/log
log/stationary
stationary/declining
declining/prolonged declining

questions.answerRationale: Enzymes (primary metabolites) are best harvested during active log-phase growth when cells are most metabolically active; antibiotics (secondary metabolites) are typically produced later, once growth slows into stationary phase.

questions.stem: A scientist wants to maintain the log phase growth condition of a strain of Escherichia coli indefinitelshould y. What the scientists do? Note: She must keep the culture uncontaminated.

options.text: Nothing, it is impossible in a closed system.
The scientist should grow the bacterium in a small pond.
The scientists should oxygenate the culture by bubbling filtered air.
The scientist should remove some culture and replenish the volume with a fresh medium.

questions.answerRationale: Continuously removing some culture and replenishing it with fresh medium (a chemostat-style approach) keeps nutrients available and waste diluted, sustaining log-phase growth indefinitely - unlike a static closed batch culture, which inevitably exits log phase as resources run out.

questions.stem: A scientist serially diluted a stool sample of a diarrhea patient in this manner: (i) Stock sample, (ii) 1 ml of stock sample+ 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (iii) 1 ml of diluted sample ii + 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (iv) 1 ml of diluted sample iii+ 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (v) 1 ml of diluted sample iv+ 9 ml of LB broth, mixed. The scientist plated 100 microliters of the diluted sample (v) on a plate. What was the dilution factor (df)?
questions.answerRationale: Three successive 1:10 dilutions from the stock (steps ii, iii, iv) compound to a 1:1,000 dilution at sample iv, and one more 1:10 step to sample v brings the total dilution factor to 1/10,000.

questions.stem: A scientist serially diluted a stool sample of a diarrhea patient in this manner: (i) Stock sample, (ii) 1 ml of stock sample + 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (iii) 1 ml of diluted sample ii + 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (iv) 1 ml of diluted sample iii+ 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (v) 1 ml of diluted sample iv+ 9 ml of LB broth, mixed. The scientist plated 100 microliters of the diluted sample iii, iv, and v on a plate and obtained 320, 34, and 5 colonies on the plates, respectively. What is the bacterial count of the stock sample? Note: make a significant colony count. Please use the formula N= (n/v) x df, where N is the bacterial count/ml of the original sample, n is the number of colonies grown in the plate, v is the volume of liquid plated and df is the dilution factor.
questions.answerRationale: The plate with a colony count in the reliably countable 30-300 range (34 colonies, from sample iv at a 1,000-fold dilution) is the one to use for calculating the stock concentration - samples iii (320, over the reliable range) and v (5, too few) are both statistically less trustworthy.

questions.stem: A600 of an E. coli culture in LB broth was 0.5. The culture is currently at the _______ phase of the growth curve.

options.text: lag
log
stationary
declining

questions.answerRationale: An OD600 of 0.5 is the standard, widely-used benchmark in molecular biology protocols for harvesting E. coli in mid-log (exponential) phase.

questions.stem: A 100 ml sample of pond water was filtered using a 0.4-micron filter paper, and the filter paper was exposed to a MacConkey agar plate. 120 bacterial colonies developed after overnight incubation of the plate. What is the bacterial count of the pond water, and what type of bacteria were counted by the protocol?

options.text: 1.20 cfu/ml, G(-) bacteria that can grow in MacConkey agar plate.
120 cfu/ ml, all types of bacteria present in the pond water.
1,200 cfu/ml, G(-) bacteria present in the pond water.

questions.answerRationale: Filtering the full 100 mL sample and counting the whole filter gives 120 colonies per 100 mL, i.e. 1.2 cfu/mL; and since MacConkey agar only supports growth of Gram-negative bacteria able to tolerate it, the count reflects that subset, not every bacterium present in the pond water.

questions.stem: A person treated a surgical knife with 10% Clorox® solution. She performed _______.

options.text: sanitizing
sterilization
disinfection
pasteurization
antisepsis

questions.answerRationale: Applying a chemical agent like bleach to an inanimate surgical instrument is disinfection - sterilization implies killing all life forms including spores, sanitizing is a lower-level reduction typically for food-contact surfaces, and antisepsis specifically applies to living tissue.

questions.stem: Pasteurization is technically comparable to which of these?

options.text: HLD.
ILD.
LLD.
UHLD.

questions.answerRationale: Pasteurization kills vegetative pathogens (including Mycobacterium) but not bacterial spores, which is the technical definition of intermediate-level disinfection (ILD).

questions.stem: Which of the following definitions is CORRECT?

options.text: Commercial Sterilization: Sufficient treatment to inactivate Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Degerming: Mechanical removal of microbes from the surface of live tissues.
Disinfection: Removal of vegetative pathogens from skin surfaces.
Antisepsis: Removal of pathogens from surfaces of utensils.
Sterilization: Removal of all vegetative cells.

questions.answerRationale: Degerming is specifically the mechanical removal of microbes from living tissue (e.g. an alcohol wipe before an injection) - disinfection applies to inanimate surfaces (not skin), antisepsis applies to living tissue (not utensils), commercial sterilization in the food industry targets Clostridium botulinum spores (not TB), and true sterilization means killing all life forms, not just vegetative cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is technically correct?

options.text: The higher the number of microbes, the faster the killing.
The higher the amount of biofilm, the faster the rate of killing.
When Mycobacterium and naked viruses are inactivated, the surface is completely disinfected.
High-intensity treatment with a short exposure time is equivalent to low-intensity treatment with a long exposure time.

questions.answerRationale: The recognized D-value/thermal-death-time principle in sterilization science holds that a shorter, more intense treatment can achieve the same lethality as a longer, milder one - unlike the false claims that higher starting numbers or more biofilm speed up killing.

questions.stem: The membrane, proteins, and DNA are the major targets for inactivating microbes. If you destroy the plasma membrane of a cellular microbe, which of the following aspects will be immediately affected?

options.text: All metabolic activities will collapse.
Biological homeostasis will collapse.
Protein synthesis and processing will collapse.
Energy (ATP) synthesis/acquisition will collapse.
Genome replication and transcription will collapse.

questions.answerRationale: Losing the plasma membrane's barrier function immediately and directly destroys the cell's ability to maintain its internal environment (homeostasis), which is the first, most direct consequence underlying the subsequent collapse of every membrane-dependent process.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a valid definition of D value?

options.text: Time of heat treatment needed to reduce the number of microbes of a sample by one log.
Intensity of treatment needed to reduce the number of microbes of a sample by 90%.
Reduction of the number of microbes of a sample to ~10 to the power 0 (i.e., 1)
Two of these definitions are valid.
All these definitions are valid.

questions.answerRationale: Reducing a population by one log (a 10-fold, i.e. 90%, reduction) is the same event described two different ways - as a TIME needed (option A) or an INTENSITY needed (option B) - so both are valid descriptions of the same D-value concept, while "reduction to ~1 organism" describes a different endpoint (near-total sterility) entirely.

questions.stem: After one D-value of treatment, the bacterial count in a batch of soup was 100,000/liter. What would be the bacterial count after three more D-value equivalents of treatment?

options.text: 1,000/liter.
100/liter.
10/liter.
0/liter.

questions.answerRationale: Each D-value is one more 10-fold reduction: 100,000 -> 10,000 -> 1,000 -> 100 after three additional D-value treatments.

questions.stem: A stainless-steel dental probe to be used in cleaning teeth should be treated with ___________ and an endoscope (made of plastic tubing) should receive a _________.

options.text: HLD/ILD
ILD/LLD
HLD/LLD
Autoclaving/HLD

questions.answerRationale: A reusable stainless-steel instrument that contacts blood/tissue can and should be autoclaved (it tolerates heat), while a heat-sensitive plastic endoscope that only contacts mucous membranes needs high-level chemical disinfection instead, since it cannot be autoclaved.

questions.stem: In theory, a tongue depressor is considered a __________ item, and a dental probe used for teeth cleaning is considered a __________ item.

options.text: critical/ semi-critical
semi-critical/ critical
non-critical/non-critical
non-critical/ semi-critical

questions.answerRationale: A tongue depressor is the classic textbook example of a low-risk, non-critical item, while a probe that causes bleeding during use is a step up in risk - contacting blood/mucous membranes without deep tissue penetration - making it semi-critical.

questions.stem: If you have killed/inactivated ___________, you might have killed/inactivated the rest of the microbes shown here.

options.text: bacterial or fungal spores
enveloped viruses
protozoan cysts
fungal hyphae
naked viruses Hand washing

questions.answerRationale: Bacterial and fungal spores sit at (or near) the top of the microbial resistance hierarchy - killing them implies everything less resistant (naked and enveloped viruses, cysts, hyphae, vegetative cells) has also been killed.

questions.stem: General hand washing is required before and after all these activities EXCEPT _________?

options.text: touching infants
preparing food and examining patients
waking up from sleep and using restrooms
touching garbage, animals, animal food, and animal waste

questions.answerRationale: "Waking up from sleep" is not a recognized handwashing trigger, unlike using the restroom (bundled into the same option), touching infants, preparing food, examining patients, or touching garbage and animals.

questions.stem: Which of the following is recommended for general handwashing?

options.text: Use bar soap.
Rinse hands after lathering.
Take soap before wetting hands.
Use a filter-free forced-air hand drier.
Lather hands thoroughly for 10 seconds.

questions.answerRationale: Correct technique is to wet hands, apply soap, lather thoroughly, and only then rinse - bar soap and filter-free air driers can spread contamination, taking soap before wetting is the wrong order, and 10 seconds of lathering falls short of the recommended ~20 seconds.

questions.stem: One should not use a hand sanitizers to clean hands if _______________.

options.text: its ingredients include triclosan or triclocarban
the alcohol content of the sanitizer is >75%
its ingredients include polyacrylate
one’s hands are visibly dirty

questions.answerRationale: Hand sanitizer cannot remove visible dirt or organic material - health guidelines are explicit that visibly soiled hands require actual soap-and-water washing instead.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of medical handwashing?

options.text: Remove all microbes from hands.
Reduce the microbe counts on hands.
Remove the environmental microbes but not the resident microbes on hand.
Remove the environmental microbes and the resident microbes that may readily shed from the hands.

questions.answerRationale: Medical handwashing is specifically meant to remove both transient environmental microbes AND the resident flora that could still be shed during patient care - going further than general handwashing, which mainly targets transient contamination.

questions.stem: Which of the following is part of medical handwashing but not general handwashing?

options.text: Using liquid hand soap.
Scrubbing for a minimum of 20 seconds.
Using iodinated soap and sponge scrubbers.
Wiping washed hands with a clean paper towel.

questions.answerRationale: Scrubbing with iodinated (antimicrobial) soap and sponge scrubbers is the hallmark of a medical/surgical scrub, a step beyond ordinary general handwashing.

questions.stem: Which of the following emblems is not expected in a BSL-3 facility?

options.text: Recycle.
Biohazard.
Broken glass.
Radioactivity.
No food or drinks.

questions.answerRationale: A recycling symbol is fundamentally inconsistent with BSL-3 practice, since all waste from such a facility must be treated as biohazardous rather than routed through normal recycling streams - unlike biohazard, broken-glass, and no-food-or-drink signage, which are all standard containment-lab warnings.

questions.stem: A physician’s assistant (PA) is about to examine a patient who is potentially HIV- and tuberculosis-positive. Which of the following items is NOT necessary for the PA to wear to protect herself and her patient?

options.text: Gloves.
Goggles.
Shoe covers.
Body garb.
Nose mask.

questions.answerRationale: Shoe covers are not part of standard precautions for a routine patient exam - gloves, goggles, a gown, and a mask (especially for a TB-suspect patient) are the actual necessary protective items.

questions.stem: A worker is about to enter a BSL-3 facility. Which of the following wearables is NOT necessary for her?

options.text: Shoe covers.
Full-face mask.
All sterile wearables.
Contained respirator suit.
Positive airflow respirator suit.

questions.answerRationale: BSL-3 PPE is about containment/barrier protection, not maintaining a sterile field, so requiring every wearable to be sterile is excessive - shoe covers, a full-face mask, and (for higher-risk work) a contained or positive-pressure respirator suit are the genuinely relevant items.

sections.heading: Biosafety containment facilities and emergency protocols

questions.stem: Which of the following is certainly a BSL-2 facility (and not a BSL-1, BSL-3, or BSL-4 facility)?

options.text: It has an eyewash station.
It has biohazard emblems posted on the door.
It has laminar flow hoods equipped with HEPA filters.
It has workbenches that are impervious to acids and bases.
Its floor and walls are made of monolithic solid impervious materials.

questions.answerRationale: Biosafety cabinets with HEPA filtration are a defining upgrade introduced at BSL-2 (absent at BSL-1), while the other options either apply across every level (eyewash stations, impervious workbenches) or describe more stringent structural containment specific to BSL-3.

questions.stem: If you want to grow Mycobacterium tuberculosis in your laboratory, your laboratory must be certified at the minimum as a BSL __________ facility, ___________ fancily must have double-entry doors.

options.text: 1/BSL 1 and BSL-2
2/ BSL-2 and BLS-3
3/ BSL 3 and BSL 4

questions.answerRationale: Growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis requires at minimum BSL-3 certification, and both BSL-3 and BSL-4 facilities are built with double-entry/airlock doors as a structural containment feature.

questions.stem: A person cut himself while cleaning a knife that was used in surgery. The person is a new hire in his probation period and had not reported that he tested positive for tuberculosis on a skin test. What should the person do?

options.text: Report the incident to the authority and deposit a blood sample.
Do not report the incident as long as the injury is not life-threatening.
Seek first aid but do not report the incident or deposit a blood sample.

questions.answerRationale: Any sharps injury must be reported immediately and a baseline blood sample taken, regardless of the employee's probationary status or how minor the injury seems - this is standard occupational exposure protocol.

sections.heading: Physical methods: Heat energy and cryopreservation

questions.stem: For what reasons is dry heat sterilization sometimes preferred to moist heat sterilization (i.e., autoclaving)?

options.text: Dry heat is faster and more efficient.
Dry heat is less expensive and thus more affordable.
Dry heat destroys the prion agents and RNase enzymes.
Dry heat is the only method of deactivating the prion agents.

questions.answerRationale: Dry heat at high temperature for extended time is specifically useful against tough contaminants like prions and RNases, a genuine practical reason to prefer it in certain applications (e.g. RNase-free glassware) - though it is not literally the ONLY method, ruling out the more absolute claim.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best practice of using inoculation loops?

options.text: Disposable plastic loops; used and then discarded.
Metal reusable loops; incinerated using a Bunsen burner before and after use.
Metal reusable loops; incinerated using a loop incinerator before and after use.

questions.answerRationale: An enclosed loop incinerator sterilizes a reusable metal loop without the open-flame aerosolization/splatter risk that comes with flaming a loaded loop directly in a Bunsen burner.

questions.stem: Which of these is needed to prepare steam heated to 121-135 °C in an autoclave or a cooking pot?

options.text: Water used must be soft, pure, and free of any suspended contaminants.
The altitude must be higher than 1,000 meters above sea level.
The pressure inside the container must be 15 PSI or higher.
The container's volume must expand when heated.

questions.answerRationale: Steam only exceeds the normal 100°C boiling point when confined under increased pressure - roughly 15 PSI above atmospheric is what allows an autoclave or pressure cooker to reach 121-135°C.

questions.stem: A lab technician is using an autoclave to sterilize a bottle of bacterial growth medium and some surgical knives. Which of the following should/could the technician do?

options.text: Wrap the knives with aluminum foil and mark the pack with heat-sensitive tape.
Open the autoclave door as soon as the treatment cycles are over.
Tightly cap the bottle containing bacterial growth medium.
Set the autoclave to operate on the liquid cycle.

questions.answerRationale: Setting the whole autoclave load to the liquid cycle (slower depressurization) is the safe choice when a bottle of liquid growth medium is included, preventing dangerous boil-over without harming the dry surgical knives also being sterilized.

questions.stem: Which of the following tests ensures that an item has been autoclaved properly?

options.text: The stripes of the autoclave tape on the item have been darkened.
The autoclave sensor printout shows that the cycles went as expected.
The color of the spore test ampules (autoclaved with the item) has not changed after two days.
The color of the spore test ampules (autoclaved with the item) has turned yellow after two days.

questions.answerRationale: A biological spore indicator that shows no growth (no color change) after incubation is the gold-standard, most definitive proof that sterilization actually killed even resistant spores - unlike indicator tape (only proves a temperature was reached) or a process printout (only proves the machine ran as programmed).

questions.stem: Food industries use the high-temperature short-time (HTST) method of pasteurizing milk. Which of the following is an HTST treatment?

options.text: Heating 63oC for 30 minutes.
Heating 72oC for 15 seconds.
Autoclaving at 121oC for 1 minute.
Heating 140-150oC for one second and then rapidly cooling down.

questions.answerRationale: Standard HTST pasteurization is defined as heating to 72°C for 15 seconds.

questions.stem: Milk is pasteurized and not autoclaved (to increase shelf life) and to____________, fish or meat is frozen before consuming raw to ________.

options.text: reduce cost of preservation/
enhance nutritional quality/ inactivate viruses and bacteria
preserve flavor and consistency/ to kill worm larvae and eggs Physical methods: Electromagnetic radiation

questions.answerRationale: Pasteurizing (rather than autoclaving) milk preserves its flavor and texture while still making it safe, and freezing raw fish or meat before eating specifically kills parasitic worm larvae and eggs that cooking would otherwise be relied on to destroy.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about electromagnetic waves is a mismatch?

options.text: Laser (visible) light: Utilizes heat to kill some bacteria in live tissues.
UV light (254 nm): Ionizes water and creates highly reactive oxygen radicals.
Microwave oven: Utilizes heat and not damaging electromagnetic radiation to kill microbes.
Gamma and X-radiation: Ionize water, the resulting free radicals cause single- and double-stranded DNA breaks.
61. Which of the following is the main reason for electron beam irradiation being preferred to gamma irradiation?

questions.answerRationale: UV light at 254 nm is non-ionizing radiation that damages DNA directly by forming pyrimidine dimers - it does not ionize water or generate reactive oxygen radicals, which is instead the mechanism of ionizing radiation like gamma and X-rays.

questions.stem: Which of the following are the most effective measures for preventing viral infections?

options.text: Vaccines approved by NIAID.
Handwashing and practicing proper personal hygiene.
Avoiding casual sex and intravenous recreational drug use.
wearing appropriate garb and using protective laboratory gears.
Food inspection, proper management of pets, pest control, and proper waste disposal.

questions.answerRationale: Vaccination is the single most broadly effective, population-level primary prevention strategy against viral disease historically (smallpox eradication, polio/measles control) - the other measures each address only one specific transmission route.

questions.stem: The spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 is the ligand that binds to ACE2 receptors on the host cell. Which of the following may, in theory, increase the rate of attachment of SARS-CoV-2 to the host cells?

options.text: An antibody that binds the spike proteins of the virus.
A drug that activates the expression of the ACE2 gene.
An antibody that binds the ACE2 proteins of the host cells.
A synthetic peptide that mimics the ACE2 protein and binds the spike protein.
A synthetic peptide that mimics the spike protein and binds the ACE2 protein.

questions.answerRationale: A drug that boosts ACE2 receptor expression would put more binding targets on host cells, increasing the rate of spike protein attachment - antibodies or decoy peptides that block either the spike or the receptor would instead reduce attachment.

sections.heading: Common antiviral drugs, their target, and mechanisms

questions.stem: Chloroquine binds to a potassium channel of the plasma membrane and interferes with membrane trafficking. Chloroquine most likely interferes with __________ of the virus replication cycle.

options.text: biosynthesis
penetration
attachment
uncoating
assembly

questions.answerRationale: Chloroquine's classic mechanism is raising endosomal pH, which disrupts the acidification needed for the virus to uncoat and release its genome after entry.

questions.stem: Amantadine binds the M proteins on the envelope of the influenza virus. Amantadine inhibits __________ of the replication cycle of influenza viruses.

options.text: biosynthesis
penetration
attachment
uncoating
assembly

questions.answerRationale: Amantadine blocks the influenza M2 ion channel, preventing the endosomal acidification needed to release the viral genome during uncoating - a classic, well-established pharmacology fact.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a good attribute of nucleotide analogs as antiviral drugs?

options.text: Nucleotide analogs make the newly synthesized DNA or RNA highly fragile.
Nucleotide analogs increase the rate of mutation in the virus genomes.
Nucleotide analogs interfere with DNA or RNA replication.
Nucleotide analogs rapidly kill susceptible host cells.

questions.answerRationale: Rapidly killing the host cells a drug is meant to protect is a toxicity liability, not a desirable feature - unlike genome fragility, increased mutation rate, and interference with replication, which are all the drug's intended antiviral mechanisms.

questions.stem: Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HART) combines two or more antiviral drugs, and the therapy is highly effective. Which of the following is NOT a good reason for adopting combination antiviral therapy?

options.text: Multiple drugs in the mixture inhibit multiple drug targets of the virus.
The drug mixture prevents rapid mutation and evolution of the virus.
The drug cocktail prevents the development of viral drug resistance.
The toxicity of the combined drugs acts synergistically.

questions.answerRationale: Synergistic toxicity (more combined harm) is a downside, not a reason to combine drugs - unlike hitting multiple targets, slowing viral evolution, and preventing resistance, which are the actual, desirable justifications for combination therapy.

questions.stem: Which of the following steps of the influenza virus replication cycle is inhibited by zanamivir?

options.text: Assembly of the nucleocapsid of the virus.
Budding of the virus particles out of the plasma membrane.
Separation of the egressed viruses from the plasma membrane of the progenitor cells.
Assembly of viral envelope glycoproteins and matrix proteins on the plasma membrane of the host cell.

questions.answerRationale: Zanamivir inhibits neuraminidase, the enzyme that cleaves sialic acid to let newly budded virus particles detach from the infected cell surface - without it, progeny viruses stay stuck to the cell.

questions.stem: Which of the following cells has the most optimal conditions to establish an antiviral state?

options.text: A cell that has secreted interferons.
A cell that has been infected by a virus.
A cell has expressed receptors for interferons.
A cell that has its interferon receptors bound to secreted interferons.

questions.answerRationale: The antiviral state is established once a cell's interferon receptors are actually bound by secreted interferon, triggering the downstream defensive gene expression - simply secreting interferon or expressing unbound receptors doesn't by itself establish the state.

questions.stem: A cell that has established an antiviral state. Which of these is not an expected activity of the cell?

options.text: Preventing transcription of viral genes or translation of viral proteins.
Replicating chromosomes and dividing by mitosis.
Destroying/modifying viral RNA and proteins.
Preventing entry or egress of the virus.
Preventing virus assembly.

questions.answerRationale: A cell mounting a defensive antiviral response generally shuts down normal macromolecular synthesis and growth to limit resources available to the virus - continuing to divide by mitosis as usual is not part of that defensive posture.

questions.stem: The following statements describe how interfering dsRNA inhibits the translation of viral mRNAs. One of the statements is INCORRECT. Which of the statements is that?

options.text: Dicer cuts the interfering dsRNA into small pieces about 25 bp.
RISC takes the 25 bp RNA fragments to use them as guide RNAs.
RISC hybridizes a guide RNA with the target mRNA of the virus.
Dicer cuts the viral mRNA that is hybridized with the guide RNA.
Ribosomes fail to translate the fragmented viral mRNA (the mRNA disintegrates).

questions.answerRationale: Dicer's job is only to chop the initial dsRNA into small guide fragments; the actual cleavage of the target viral mRNA (once paired with the guide strand inside RISC) is carried out by Argonaute's slicer activity, not by Dicer again.

questions.stem: RNA interference (RNAi) drugs have been approved for treating certain diseases. Which of the following is the most pressing problem of RNAi therapy?

options.text: Problem with the stability of dsRNA molecules.
Synthesis and packing of dsRNA and efficacy of the drug.
Healthy cells receiving the dsRNA (i.e., synthesis of excess interferons).
Delivery of dsRNA inside the target cells in the specific tissues of specific organs.

questions.answerRationale: Delivering RNAi drugs specifically into the right cells within the right tissue of the right organ remains the most persistent, unsolved bottleneck for RNAi therapeutics, more so than dsRNA stability, synthesis, or off-target immune activation, which have all seen more progress.

questions.stem: Passive immunization (i.e., injecting specific antibodies) targets mainly the _______ step of the virus replication cycle.

options.text: biosynthesis
penetration
attachment
assembly
egress

questions.answerRationale: Antibodies primarily work by binding and neutralizing free virus particles before they can attach to a new host cell.

questions.stem: Which of the following antibodies has no use in preventing or treating SARS CoV-2 infections?

options.text: Anti-SARS CoV-2 IgG antibodies separated from all other proteins in the plasma of a donor.
Serum of volunteers who have never been infected by the virus.
Serum of a healthy horse experimentally infected by the virus.
Whole serum of a person previously infected by the virus.

questions.answerRationale: Serum from someone never infected (and presumably unvaccinated) contains no anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies at all, making it useless for passive immunization - unlike purified IgG, convalescent (previously-infected) serum, or antiserum raised in another animal, all of which do contain the needed antibodies.

questions.stem: An antimicrobial chemotherapeutic agent should be a magic bullet. What does a magic bullet do?

options.text: It would kill/inactivate microbes effectively.
It would be harmless to the host organism.
It would be harmless to the resident biota.
It would have all these attributes

questions.answerRationale: Paul Ehrlich's original "magic bullet" concept specifically combined all three properties at once: killing the pathogen effectively, while being harmless to both the host and its normal microbiota.

questions.stem: The first antimicrobial chemotherapeutic agent with the properties of a magic bullet that was applied to treat bacterial infections in humans was__________ and it was developed by ___________.

options.text: salvarsan/ Paul Ehrlich (1854-1915)
prontosil/ Gerhard Domagk (1895-1964)
penicillin/ Alexander Fleming (1885-1955)
streptomycin/ Selman Waxman (1888-1973)

questions.answerRationale: Salvarsan, developed by Paul Ehrlich, was the first true "magic bullet" synthetic chemotherapeutic agent, used to treat syphilis, predating both sulfa drugs and penicillin.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most suitable target for developing antibacterial chemotherapeutic agents?

options.text: Lipid synthesis and membrane dynamics.
Cell wall synthesis and maintenance.
DNA replication and recombination.
RNA transcription and processing.
Protein synthesis and processing.

questions.answerRationale: The bacterial cell wall is the gold-standard example of selective toxicity, since human cells have no cell wall at all - making it the safest, most bacteria-specific drug target of the options listed.

questions.stem: Why bacterial DNA replication is not an ideal target for developing antibacterial drugs.

options.text: No known agent inhibits bacterial DNA polymerase.
DNA replication in bacteria and human cells has many similarities.
Agents that may inhibit bacterial DNA replication are potential mutagens.
Agents that inhibit bacterial DNA replication cannot penetrate the bacterial cell wall.

questions.answerRationale: Bacterial and human DNA replication machinery share substantial mechanistic similarity, making it hard to hit bacterial replication selectively without also damaging the host's own replication - unlike the cell wall, which is entirely absent in human cells.

questions.stem: Why are membrane-active antibiotics such as polymyxins, daptomycin, and gramicidin usually used in treating surface wounds and not as orally and parenterally (injected) administered drugs? Note: Only the best answer will be scored.

options.text: The drugs are not absorbed if taken orally or injected.
The drugs may damage the host cell’s membranes.
The drugs are made of a polypeptide and a lipid.

questions.answerRationale: Because these drugs act on membranes - a feature bacterial and host cells share far more than the bacteria-specific cell wall - they carry real toxicity risk (e.g. nephrotoxicity) if given systemically, which is why they're mostly restricted to topical/localized use.

questions.stem: Isoniazid and ethionamide inhibit mycolic acid synthesis; thus, they are effective against _______________.

options.text: all actinobacteria
acid-fast bacteria
broad range of bacteria
bacteria lacking a cell wall Antibacterials: Beta-lactams

questions.answerRationale: Mycolic acid is precisely what makes a bacterium "acid-fast," so a mycolic-acid-synthesis inhibitor is specifically effective against acid-fast organisms, not actinobacteria broadly or bacteria in general.

questions.stem: Which reactions or processes of bacterial cell wall synthesis do beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit?

options.text: Synthesis of polyalanine oligopeptides.
Synthesis of the NAG-NAM disaccharide.
Attachment of NAG-NAM disaccharide to an existing polysaccharide.
Cross-linking of two amino acids of the oligopeptides of two NAM entities.
Transport of NAG-NAM disaccharide units outside of the plasma membrane.

questions.answerRationale: Beta-lactams inhibit penicillin-binding proteins' transpeptidase activity - the final step crosslinking peptide chains between adjacent NAM units of the peptidoglycan.

questions.stem: Why do many physicians prefer amoxicillin-clavulanate to amoxicillin in treating bacterial infections?

options.text: Clavulanate inhibits beta-lactamases.
Clavulanate inhibits bacterial transpeptidase.
Clavulanate reduces the toxicity of amoxicillin.
Clavulanate increases the bioavailability of amoxicillin.

questions.answerRationale: Clavulanate itself has little antibacterial activity but inhibits bacterial beta-lactamase enzymes, protecting amoxicillin from being degraded by resistant strains.

questions.stem: A strain of Staphylococcus aureus became resistant to methicillin because it produces a beta-lactamase enzyme. How does the beta-lactamase enzyme make the bacterium methicillin-resistant?

options.text: The enzyme cuts open the thiazolidine ring of methicillin.
The enzyme cuts C-N bond and opens the beta-lactam ring of methicillin.
The enzyme binds methicillin and prevents transpeptidases from binding the antibiotics.
The enzyme chemically modifies methicillin by attaching a methyl group to the beta-lactamase ring.

questions.answerRationale: Beta-lactamase enzymes work by hydrolyzing the C-N bond within the beta-lactam ring itself, destroying the ring's ability to bind and inhibit penicillin-binding proteins.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a purpose of designing semi-synthetic or fully synthetic antibiotics?

options.text: Reduce drug toxicity.
Reduce drug bioavailability.
Making the drugs broad-spectrum.
Making the drugs resistant to bacterial enzymes.

questions.answerRationale: Reducing bioavailability would make a drug worse, not better - designers actually aim to increase bioavailability, alongside reducing toxicity, broadening spectrum, and evading bacterial resistance enzymes.

questions.stem: Which of the following antibiotics can be used in treating Mycoplasma pneumoniae?

options.text: Cephalosporins or cephamycins (3rd, 4th or 5th generation).
Aminopenicillins such as carbenicillin.
Monobactams such as meropenem.
Fully synthetic carbapenems.
None of these antibiotics.

questions.answerRationale: Mycoplasma pneumoniae has no cell wall at all, so every option listed here (cephalosporins, aminopenicillins, monobactams, carbapenems) - all beta-lactam, cell-wall-targeting drugs - has no target to act on and is completely ineffective.

sections.heading: Other inhibitors of cell wall synthesis

questions.stem: Which of these statements about vancomycin is INCORRECT?

options.text: It is made of amino acids and sugars.
It is only effective against G(+) bacteria.
It is effective against MERSA and VERSA.
It prevents the crosslinking of oligopeptides of the bacterial cell wall.
It is effective against the naturally drug-resistant soil bacterium Clostridium difficile.

questions.answerRationale: VRSA is, by definition, Vancomycin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus - claiming vancomycin is effective against it is a direct contradiction, unlike the other true statements about vancomycin's composition, Gram-positive specificity, crosslinking-blocking mechanism, and use against C. difficile.

questions.stem: Ethambutol inhibits arabinogalactan synthesis. Which of the bacteria should the drug be effective against?

options.text: G(+) bacteria such as actinobacteria.
G(-) bacteria such as proteobacteria.
G(-) bacteria such as mycoplasmas.
Spirochetes.

questions.answerRationale: Arabinogalactan is a component specifically of the mycobacterial (Actinobacteria) cell wall, so a drug targeting its synthesis is effective against that group specifically.

questions.stem: Cycloserine is related to a/an________, and it is used as a second line of antibiotics to treat__________ if other antibiotics do not work.

options.text: fatty acid/ anaerobic bacterial infections of soft tissues
amino acid/multidrug-resistant mycobacteria
nucleotide/ disseminated bacterial infections
monosaccharide/ mixed bacterial infections Inhibitors of DNA replication

questions.answerRationale: Cycloserine is a D-alanine (amino acid) analog used as a second-line drug for multidrug-resistant mycobacterial (TB) infections.

questions.stem: How do fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA replication in bacteria?

options.text: They inhibit bacterial helicase.
They inhibit bacterial DNA polymerase.
They inhibit bacterial DNA topoisomerase.
They inhibit the bacterial DNA sliding clamp.

questions.answerRationale: Fluoroquinolones specifically target bacterial DNA gyrase, a type II topoisomerase needed to manage DNA supercoiling during replication.

questions.stem: Metronidazole binds to DNA and causes single-stranded DNA breaks. Why is this a medical concern, and why is the drug effective only against anaerobic bacteria and protozoa?

options.text: The drug may create drug-resistant bacteria; aerobes do not absorb the drug.
A high dose of the drug is necessary to make the drug effective; oxygen destroys the drug.
The drug may mutate the host cell’s chromosomes; only anaerobes have nitroreductase to activate the drug.

questions.answerRationale: Metronidazole is a prodrug that must be activated by nitroreductase, an enzyme found specifically in anaerobic organisms - explaining both its anaerobe-only selectivity and the genotoxicity concern once the activated form damages DNA.

questions.stem: Clofazimine, one of the most effective drugs to treat leprosy, binds guanine residues. Which of these bacterial activities does the drug directly affect?

options.text: Lipid synthesis
DNA replication.
RNA transcription.
Protein synthesis and processing.

questions.answerRationale: A compound that binds directly to DNA guanine bases most classically interferes with RNA polymerase reading through the DNA template, the textbook mechanism shared by other DNA-intercalating transcription inhibitors like actinomycin D.

questions.stem: Mutations in which of these genes would make a bacterium resistant to rifamycin, and why is rifamycin always used in combination therapy?

options.text: The DNA polymerase gene; the drug is highly toxic.
The DNA helicase gene, the drug is unstable if used alone.
The RNA polymerase gene; bacteria readily become resistant to the drug.

questions.answerRationale: Rifamycin targets bacterial RNA polymerase directly, so mutations in that gene's sequence confer resistance; bacteria are also well known to develop rifamycin resistance quickly when it is used alone, which is why it is never given as monotherapy.

questions.stem: Aminoglycosides bind the 23S rRNA of the 30S ribosome particles. Which of the following steps of protein synthesis do aminoglycosides most likely inhibit?

options.text: Translation initiation.
Translation elongation.
Translation termination.
Post-termination event (such as ribosome recycling).

questions.answerRationale: Aminoglycosides are classically taught to cause misreading of the genetic code during the elongation phase of translation, leading to mistranslated, nonfunctional proteins.

questions.stem: (a) Which of the following aminoglycosides is nontoxic, and (b) which of the aminoglycosides is used in treating/preventing Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections of the lung of cystic fibrosis patients?

options.text: (a) Kanamycin/(b) Neomycin.
(a) Neomycin/ (b) Streptomycin.
(a) Streptomycin/ (b) gentamycin.
(a) Streptomycin/ (b) Plazomicin.
(a) None of the aminoglycosides/ (b) Tobramycin.

questions.answerRationale: Every aminoglycoside carries meaningful nephro/ototoxicity risk, so "none are truly nontoxic" is the accurate pharmacological answer for part (a); inhaled tobramycin is the well-established, specific choice for treating/preventing Pseudomonas aeruginosa lung infections in cystic fibrosis patients.

sections.heading: Inhibitors of protein synthesis: Tetracyclines and macrolides

questions.stem: All tetracyclines have a __________ structure, and of the tetracyclines, __________ is often used in treating sexually transmitted and intracellular bacterial pathogens.

options.text: polyketide/ doxycycline
macrocyclic ring/ minocycline
cyclobutene ring/ chlortetracycline

questions.answerRationale: Tetracyclines share a common polyketide-derived four-ring core structure, and doxycycline is the standard tetracycline used for sexually transmitted and intracellular pathogens like Chlamydia and Rickettsia.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about tetracycline is INCORRECT?

options.text: Tetracyclines are narrow-spectrum antibiotics.
Tetracyclines become more toxic after the expiration date.
Tetracyclines deposit in the bones and can be teratogenic to fetuses.
The drugs bind 16S RNA of 30S ribosome, but they probably also bind 50S ribosomes.
Some tetracyclines are used in treating autoimmune diseases (the drugs are immunosuppressive)

questions.answerRationale: Tetracyclines are actually well-known broad-spectrum antibiotics, active against a wide range of Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and atypical organisms - calling them narrow-spectrum is the false statement here.

questions.stem: Macrolides, such as azithromycin, bind 23S rRNA, thus they bind _________ and prevent bacterial translation elongation.

options.text: 30S ribosomes
40S ribosomes
50S ribosomes Inhibitors of protein synthesis: other protein synthesis inhibiting antibiotics

questions.answerRationale: 23S rRNA is a structural component of the large (50S) ribosomal subunit, not the 30S or a eukaryotic 40S subunit.

questions.stem: To treat MERSA and VERSA infections, one would prefer ___________; and to treat bacterial meningitis, one would prefer _________.

options.text: oxazolidines (such as linezolid)/ chloramphenicol
chloramphenicol/ lincosamides (such as clindamycin)
lincosamides (such as clindamycin)/ streptogramins such as Synercid Inhibitors of folate synthesis

questions.answerRationale: Oxazolidinones like linezolid are a go-to choice against resistant Gram-positives like MRSA/VRSA, and chloramphenicol's well-known ability to cross the blood-brain barrier makes it a classic choice for bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: Folates are vitamins ______, and they are essential for the synthesis of _________.

options.text: A/ DNA
B6/ RNA
B12/ protein
B9/ nucleotides and some amino acids

questions.answerRationale: Folate is vitamin B9, essential for synthesizing nucleotides and certain amino acids via one-carbon metabolism.

questions.stem: Sulfa drugs are structural analogs of the cellular molecule____________, and they bind the enzyme ____________.

options.text: para-amino salicylic acid (PAS)/ dihydrofolate synthase
para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) / dihydrofolate synthase
gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)/ dihydrofolate reductase
monosodium glutamate (MSG)/ gamma glutamyl transpeptidase

questions.answerRationale: Sulfonamides are structural analogs of PABA and competitively block the folate-synthesis enzyme pathway at the dihydropteroate/dihydrofolate synthesis step - trimethoprim, not sulfa drugs, is the one that targets dihydrofolate reductase specifically.

questions.stem: The commonly prescribed drug BactrimTM contains __________, while ________ are used in combination with rifampin to treat tuberculosis and leprosy.

options.text: Dapsone and PASER/ Sulfamethoxazole and chloroquine
sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim/ Dapsone or PASER
sulphathiazole and chloroquine/ trimethoprim and Dapsone

questions.answerRationale: BactrimTM is the well-known brand combining sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim; dapsone or PASER are the drugs paired with rifampin for treating leprosy and tuberculosis respectively.

questions.stem: Why are sulfa drugs and trimethoprim almost always used in combination to treat bacterial infections and as prophylaxis for pneumocystis pneumonia?

options.text: Because the two drugs inhibit two enzymes in the same metabolic pathway.
Because the two drugs are totally ineffective if used alone.
Because the two drugs act synergistically.
Because of two of these reasons.
Because of all these reasons.

questions.answerRationale: Sulfa drugs and trimethoprim block two sequential enzymes in the same folate-synthesis pathway, which is both why they act synergistically and why they're described as targeting the same pathway - both A and C describe the same underlying reality, making "two of these reasons" the accurate answer.

sections.heading: Prevention and cure of fungal infections

questions.stem: One would avoid _______ to avoid aflatoxin (a carcinogen), and _________ to avoid amatoxin (an inhibitors of RNA polymerase II).

options.text: uninspected nut and nut oil/ unidentified wild mushroom
bread made of infected rye/ contaminated dry fruits, grain, and pork
contaminated cereal grain/ partially rotted fruits, and contaminated fruit juice

questions.answerRationale: Aflatoxin classically contaminates uninspected nuts (Aspergillus flavus), and amatoxin is the toxin famously found in unidentified wild mushrooms like the death cap.

questions.stem: Of the antifungal therapeutic agents, __________ group inhibits fungal polysaccharide synthesis, and _______ inhibit ergosterol synthesis __________.

options.text: echinocandins/ allylamines
flucytosine/ griseofulvin
polyenes/ flucytosine
allylamines/ azoles
azole/polyenes

questions.answerRationale: Echinocandins inhibit beta-glucan synthase, blocking fungal cell-wall polysaccharide synthesis; allylamines like terbinafine block an earlier step of ergosterol biosynthesis (squalene epoxidase).

questions.stem: All these drugs inhibit ergosterol synthesis EXCEPT _______, it binds the ergosterol and disrupts fungal membranes.

options.text: terbinafine
fluconazole
voriconazole
ketokonazole
ampotericin B

questions.answerRationale: Amphotericin B is a polyene that directly binds existing ergosterol in the fungal membrane and punches pores in it, rather than inhibiting ergosterol's synthesis the way the azoles and terbinafine do.

questions.stem: Sordarin, an experimental drug based on a fungal metabolite. Why is the drug called a broad-spectrum antifungal drug?

options.text: Because it inhibits fungal protein synthesis
Because it is effective against yeast and mold forms of fungi
Because it is derived from a fungal metabolite, but it is an antifungal agent.

questions.answerRationale: Sordarin targets fungal translation elongation factor eEF2, a protein-synthesis component that is relatively conserved across many different fungal species, which is the mechanistic reason it has broad activity across yeasts and molds alike.

questions.stem: Which of these lessons do antiprotozoal drugs give to drug developers?

options.text: Modern science has won the war on infectious diseases.
Traditional drugs should be considered for rational drug development.
Protozoan infections are a public health problem only in the least developed countries.
There are only a few antiprotozoal drugs developed because only a few people get infected by the agents.

questions.answerRationale: Antiprotozoal chemotherapy has historically drawn heavily on older, even historically ancient remedies and heavy-metal compounds, illustrating that revisiting traditional treatments can be a legitimate, rational strategy for modern drug development.

questions.stem: All these antibacterial or antifungal agents are used in treating some protozoan infections. Which of these inhibits the DNA replication of some protozoans?

options.text: Pentamidine, metronidazole, and quinolones.
Clindamycin, tetracycline, and doxycycline.
Macrolides such as azithromycin.
Trimethoprim and sulfonamide.
Azoles and amphotericin B.

questions.answerRationale: Metronidazole directly damages DNA via strand breaks in susceptible anaerobic protozoa, and quinolones inhibit the DNA gyrase/topoisomerase enzymes needed for replication - both genuinely interfere with DNA replication, unlike the other options, which target protein synthesis or folate/ergosterol pathways.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is CORRECT about heavy metal (arsenic and antimony) organic compounds used in treating protozoan infections?

options.text: The metal ions in the drugs primarily act by inducing oxidative damage to the enzymes of the target parasites.
The drugs are used to treat amebiasis (gastroenteritis) and trichomoniasis (vaginosis).
Bismuth salicylate is an effective antiprotozoal drug.
The drugs have only modest side effects.

questions.answerRationale: Heavy-metal antiparasitic compounds (arsenic, antimony) are generally understood to act by causing oxidative damage to parasite enzymes - the other options misattribute their use (amebiasis/trichomoniasis are treated with metronidazole, not these metals), overstate bismuth salicylate's antiprotozoal efficacy, or wrongly downplay their well-documented severe toxicity.

questions.stem: All these activities expose one to worm infections. Which of these guarantees worm infections?

options.text: Consuming (unfrozen and uncooked) wild animal meat raw.
Consuming salted, smoked, or frozen uncooked food.
Worming pet animals after adopting.
Walking barefoot on sand and soil.
Wading in lakes and shallow seas.

questions.answerRationale: Raw, unfrozen wild animal meat with no preservation processing at all carries the highest, least-mitigated risk - salting, smoking, and freezing are all recognized measures that actually kill many parasitic larvae, reducing (not guaranteeing) risk.

questions.stem: Which of these anthelmintic drugs directly or indirectly paralyzes worms?

options.text: Ivermectin and pyrantel pamoate.
Albendazole and praziquantel.
Piperazine citrate and mebendazole.
Niclosamide and bithionol.
All these drugs.

questions.answerRationale: Ivermectin and pyrantel pamoate both act primarily through paralysis - ivermectin via glutamate-gated chloride channels, pyrantel pamoate as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker - unlike albendazole/mebendazole, whose mechanism is disrupting microtubules and glucose uptake rather than paralysis.

questions.stem: A veterinarian should not use _________ to treat flatworm infections and ________ in treating roundworm infections.

options.text: pyrantel pamoate/ niclosamide
piperazine citrate/ praziquantel
ivermectin/ albendazole

questions.answerRationale: Piperazine citrate is a roundworm-specific neuromuscular drug that will not work on flatworms, and praziquantel is a flatworm-specific drug (effective against both cestodes and trematodes) that is not effective against nematodes/roundworms.

questions.stem: A child is heavily infected with roundworms. Which of these is NOT a concern about this child while being treated for the infection in a clinic?

options.text: Allergic reactions to antigens released by the affected worms.
Movement of the worms may cause perforation of the intestine.
Accumulation of paralyzed worms may obstruct the intestine.
Uncontrolled muscle twitches in the child.

questions.answerRationale: Anthelmintics are selectively toxic to worm neuromuscular physiology, which differs pharmacologically from the child's own - uncontrolled muscle twitches in the child themselves would not be an expected effect of a properly selective drug, unlike allergic reactions to dying-worm antigens, intestinal perforation from worm movement, or obstruction from a mass of paralyzed worms.

questions.stem: Which of these is drug synergy?

options.text: Additive efficacy and additive side effects.
Greater than additive efficacy but less than additive drug side effects.
Greater than additive efficacy and possibly greater than additive drug side effects.

questions.answerRationale: The strict pharmacological definition of synergy is about the therapeutic EFFICACY exceeding what simple addition would predict - it says nothing guaranteed about side effects, which could go either way, unlike the more optimistic (and less accurate) claim that synergy always means reduced combined toxicity.

questions.stem: Challenge Question: Which of the following antibiotic combinations is expected to be antagonistic?

options.text: Sulfa drugs and trimethoprim.
Methicillin (a beta-lactam antibiotic) and amikacin (an aminoglycoside).
Amoxycillin (a beta-lactam antibiotic) and chloramphenicol (protein synthesis inhibitor).

questions.answerRationale: Amoxicillin (a bactericidal cell-wall-active drug that needs active bacterial growth/division to kill) combined with chloramphenicol (a bacteriostatic drug that halts growth) is the classic textbook antagonistic pairing - stopping growth removes the very condition the beta-lactam needs to work.

questions.stem: Which of these is not a reason for combination therapy?

options.text: To aim at multiple targets of difficult-to-treat pathogens.
The drugs take advantage of the synergistic effect.
To use one drug to activate another (pro)drug.
To prevent bacterial drug resistance.

questions.answerRationale: Using one drug specifically to chemically activate another prodrug is not among the standard, commonly-cited reasons for combination antimicrobial therapy - unlike hitting multiple targets, exploiting synergy, and preventing resistance, which are all textbook-standard rationales.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a drug toxicity, not a drug interaction?

options.text: Drug S binds to a plasma protein, increasing the blood level of the enzyme in the patient.
Drug R does not work if the patient drinks orange juice or a liquid antacid.
Drug Q increases the toxicity of drug Y if taken simultaneously.
Drug P reduces the efficacy of drug Y if taken simultaneously.
Drug T makes a person allergic to lip gloss and sunblock.

questions.answerRationale: A drug causing its own adverse reaction (like photosensitivity to sunlight while wearing lip gloss/sunblock) is a toxicity/side effect of that drug alone, not a drug-drug interaction - unlike the other options, which all describe one drug's effect changing because of another drug or substance.

questions.stem: The MIC of an antibiotic is 20 micrograms/kg, which of the following is most likely the MBC for the same drug?

options.text: 20 micrograms/kg.
Less than 20 micrograms/kg.
More than 20 micrograms/kg.
It cannot be predicted from the information given.

questions.answerRationale: MBC (the concentration needed to actually kill bacteria) is by definition always equal to or greater than MIC (the concentration needed merely to inhibit growth).

questions.stem: Which of the following is INCORRECT about the Kirby-Bauer test for antibiotic susceptibility?

options.text: The test can be used to determine MBC but not MIC.
The test can only be done if an antibiotic is water-soluble.
The test can only be done if an antibiotic is stable in agar media.
It can test many antibiotics at once, but only on one bacterial strain at a time.
The zone of inhibition in the test indicates if a bacterium is sensitive or resistant to an antibiotic.

questions.answerRationale: The Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion test determines susceptibility category (and can estimate MIC via correlation charts) - it does not measure MBC at all, which requires separate quantitative broth/subculture methods, making this statement backwards.

questions.stem: A strain of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic to which it was once sensitive through each of the following processes. Which of the processes involves covalent drug modification?

options.text: The strain overexpresses efflux pump proteins.
The stain has a mutation in its rRNA gene or RNA polymerase gene.
The strain suppresses the synthesis of proteins that imports drug inside the cell.
The strain expresses a modified version (the second copy) of the target protein gene.
The strain expresses an enzyme that attaches an acetyl (CH3CO) group to an antibiotic.

questions.answerRationale: An enzyme that covalently attaches an acetyl group directly onto the antibiotic molecule is a textbook example of covalent drug modification, unlike efflux pumps, target mutations, or reduced drug import, which alter access or target rather than the drug molecule itself.

questions.stem: Challenge question: Which of the following mutations would make a bacterial strain resistant to aminoglycosides?

options.text: A mutation in the 16S rRNA gene.
A mutation in the 23S rRNA gene.
A mutation in the RNA polymerase gene.
A mutation in the DNA gyrase enzyme gene.
A mutation in the dihydrofolate synthase gene.

questions.answerRationale: Aminoglycosides bind 16S rRNA within the 30S ribosomal subunit, so a mutation there directly alters the drug's binding site and confers resistance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most rapid method of spreading bacterial antibiotic resistance among different strains and species of pathogenic and nonpathogenic bacteria?

options.text: Gene mutations and vertical gene transfer.
Lateral gene transfer via bacterial conjugation.
Lateral gene transfer via bacterial transduction.
Lateral gene transfer via bacterial transformation.

questions.answerRationale: Conjugative plasmids, especially broad-host-range ones, transfer resistance genes efficiently across diverse bacterial species and strains, making conjugation the most rapid and significant driver of antibiotic resistance spread in clinical settings - more so than transduction (limited by phage host range) or transformation (limited to naturally competent species).

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely the primary reason for bacterial antibiotic resistance in the developed countries of East Asia, Western Europe, Australia, and North America?

options.text: Use of antibiotics in treating non-bacterial infections.
Patient’s ability to purchase antibiotics without prescriptions.
Use of antibiotics in animal feed and fermentation industries.
Use of improper doses of antibiotics and use of expired/outdated antibiotics.

questions.answerRationale: Widespread subtherapeutic antibiotic use in industrial livestock and fermentation industries is a major, well-documented driver of resistance in developed nations, which typically otherwise enforce prescription requirements strictly (unlike less-regulated markets where over-the-counter purchase is the bigger issue).

questions.stem: According to the WHO, bacterial antibiotic resistance is currently at a crisis point, or human civilization is already in the post-antibiotic era. Which of the following is the most critical step nations would take to overcome this crisis?

options.text: Minimize antibiotic use.
Inactivate antibiotics before disposal.
Develop new and more effective antibiotics.
Stop agricultural and industrial use of antibiotics.
Rigorously enforce the drug laws and increase public education on antibiotic use.

questions.answerRationale: Rigorous enforcement of prescribing/dispensing rules combined with public education addresses the root behavioral causes of antibiotic misuse across both healthcare systems and the public - a more comprehensive, systemic fix than narrower single-sector measures like just developing new drugs or restricting one usage sector.
